nodes.name: Point-Slope Form
nodes.statement_display:
Let $P_1=(x_1,y_1)$ be a point in the Euclidean plane and let
$m\in\mathbb{R}$. The point-slope form of the line through $P_1$ with slope
$m$ is
\[
  y-y_1=m(x-x_1).
\]
nodes.statement_tex:

\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For every point $P_1=(x_1,y_1)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and every
$m\in\mathbb{R}$, the corresponding line is the set of all
$(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfying $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The equation records all points whose slope relative to $P_1$ is $m$.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formula is obtained by setting the slope from $P_1$ to an arbitrary point
$(x,y)$ equal to $m$.

nodes.name: Two-Point Form
nodes.statement_display:
Let $P_1=(x_1,y_1)$ and $P_2=(x_2,y_2)$ be distinct points with
$x_1\neq x_2$. The two-point form of the line through $P_1$ and $P_2$ is
\[
  y-y_1=\left(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\right)(x-x_1).
\]

$x_1\neq x_2$. The two-point form of the line through $P_1$ and $P_2$ is
\[
  y-y_1=\left(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\right)(x-x_1).
\]

\]

nodes.name: General Linear Form
nodes.statement_display:
The general linear form of a line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is
\[
  Ax+By+C=0,
\]
where $A,B,C\in\mathbb{R}$ and $A^2+B^2\neq 0$.

nodes.name: Vector Parametric Form

\]
where $\mathbf r_0\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is a point on the line and
$\mathbf v\in\mathbb{R}^2$ is a nonzero direction vector.

nodes.name: Intercept Form
nodes.statement_display:
If a line meets the $x$-axis at $(a,0)$ and the $y$-axis at $(0,b)$ with
$a,b\neq 0$, its intercept form is
\[
  \frac{x}{a}+\frac{y}{b}=1.
\]

nodes.name: Affine Parametric Line in $\mathbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement_display:
Given distinct points $\mathbf x_1,\mathbf x_2\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the line
through them is
\[
  \mathbf x(t)=\mathbf x_1+t(\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1),
  \qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]

  \qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For all distinct $\mathbf x_1,\mathbf x_2\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the set
$\{\mathbf x_1+t(\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1):t\in\mathbb{R}\}$ is the affine
line through $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The parameter $t$ moves through the point $\mathbf x_1$ in the direction
$\mathbf x_2-\mathbf x_1$.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
For $0\le t\le 1$, the same formula describes the line segment joining
$\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2$. For arbitrary real $t$, it describes the
entire affine line.

nodes.name: Normal Form
nodes.statement_display:
A line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ may be written in normal form as
\[
  x\cos\alpha+y\sin\alpha-p=0,
\]
where $p\ge 0$ is the distance from the origin to the line.

nodes.name: Symmetric Form
nodes.statement_display:
Given a point $(x_1,y_1)$ and direction cosines
$(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, the symmetric form of a line is
\[
  \frac{x-x_1}{\cos\theta}
  =
  \frac{y-y_1}{\sin\theta}
  =
  r.
\]

the triangle are equal to two right angles.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Common notions are general principles of reasoning rather than specifically
geometric assumptions. They express basic behavior of equality, comparison, and
logical transfer: equal things may be substituted for equal things, adding or
subtracting equals preserves equality, and a whole exceeds its part.

Because these principles are not tied to points, lines, circles, or planes,
they can be used throughout mathematics, not only in geometry. In modern
language, they play the role of background axioms governing how equality and
comparison may be used inside proofs.

nodes.name: Quadrilateral classes
nodes.statement_display:
Of quadrilateral figures, a square is that which is both equilateral and
right-angled; an oblong that which is right-angled but not equilateral; a
rhombus that which is equilateral but not right-angled; and a rhomboid that
which has its opposite sides and angles equal to one another but is neither
equilateral nor right-angled. And let quadrilaterals other than these be called
trapezia.

\frac{\operatorname{adj}(T_1,\theta)}{\operatorname{hyp}(T_1)}

\]

nodes.statement_display:

\]
and one full turn returns the same sine and cosine values.

  =2\cos^2\theta-1
  =1-2\sin^2\theta.
\]

nodes.name: Inverse cosecant
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{inverse cosecant} function is the inverse of cosecant after cosecant
is restricted to $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\setminus\{0\}$. It is denoted by $\operatorname{arccsc}$
or $\csc^{-1}$ and has domain $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$ and range
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\setminus\{0\}$.
\[
  \operatorname{arccsc} x=\theta
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \csc\theta=x
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  -\frac{\pi}{2}\leq\theta\leq\frac{\pi}{2},\ \theta\neq 0.
\]

The \emph{inverse secant} function is the inverse of secant after secant is
restricted to $[0,\pi]\setminus\{\pi/2\}$. It is denoted by $\operatorname{arcsec}$ or
$\sec^{-1}$ and has domain $(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$ and range
$[0,\pi]\setminus\{\pi/2\}$.
\[
  \operatorname{arcsec} x=\theta
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \sec\theta=x
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  0\leq\theta\leq\pi,\ \theta\neq\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

nodes.name: Inverse sine
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{inverse sine} function is the inverse of sine after sine is
restricted to the interval
\[
  \left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right].
\]
It is denoted by $\arcsin$ or $\sin^{-1}$ and has domain $[-1,1]$ and range
$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.
\[
  \arcsin x=\theta
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \sin\theta=x
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  -\frac{\pi}{2}\leq\theta\leq\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
By the exponential form,
\[
  \cosh t=\frac{e^t+e^{-t}}{2},
  \qquad
  \sinh t=\frac{e^t-e^{-t}}{2}.
\]
The exponential function is continuous, $t\mapsto -t$ is continuous, and sums,
differences, scalar multiples, and compositions of continuous functions are
continuous. Hence $\sinh$ and $\cosh$ are continuous on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

$\mathbb{R}$, and $\operatorname{coth}$ and $\operatorname{csch}$ are
continuous on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$.
depends_on_titles: Continuity of hyperbolic sine and cosine

support_blocks.title: Interpretation

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
The functions $\tanh$ and $\operatorname{sech}$ are quotients of continuous
functions by $\cosh t$, and $\cosh t\geq 1$, so the denominator never
vanishes. The functions $\operatorname{coth}$ and $\operatorname{csch}$ are
quotients by $\sinh t$, and $\sinh t=0$ exactly at $t=0$. The quotient rule
for continuous functions gives the stated domains of continuity.

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Differentiate the exponential forms:
\[
  \frac{d}{dt}\sinh t
  =\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{e^t-e^{-t}}{2}\right)
  =\frac{e^t+e^{-t}}{2}
  =\cosh t,
\]
and
\[
  \frac{d}{dt}\cosh t
  =\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{e^t+e^{-t}}{2}\right)
  =\frac{e^t-e^{-t}}{2}
  =\sinh t.
\]
This uses linearity of differentiation and the chain rule applied to
$e^{-t}$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Use the quotient rule on $\tanh t=\sinh t/\cosh t$:
\[
  \frac{d}{dt}\tanh t
  =
  \frac{\cosh^2 t-\sinh^2 t}{\cosh^2 t}
  =
  \frac{1}{\cosh^2 t}
  =
  \operatorname{sech}^2 t.
\]
The identity $\operatorname{sech}^2 t=1-\tanh^2 t$ follows by dividing
$\cosh^2 t-\sinh^2 t=1$ by $\cosh^2 t$.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic sector
nodes.statement_display:

$x^2-y^2=1$, write
\[
  \operatorname{HArea}(O,V,P)
\]
for the signed area of the region bounded by the segment $OV$, the segment
$OP$, and the hyperbolic arc from $V$ to $P$. The sign is positive on the
upper branch and negative on the lower branch.

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Let $u=\cosh t$ and $v=\sinh t$. The identity $u^2-v^2=1$ gives
\[
  (u-v)(u+v)=1.
\]
On the right branch, $u+v>0$, so there is a unique real number $s$ such that
$u+v=e^s$. Then $u-v=e^{-s}$, and solving the two linear equations gives
\[
  u=\frac{e^s+e^{-s}}{2},
  \qquad
  v=\frac{e^s-e^{-s}}{2}.
\]
For the exponential parametrization
\[

Let $u=\cosh t$ and $v=\sinh t$. The identity $u^2-v^2=1$ gives
\[

\[

  v=\frac{e^s-e^{-s}}{2}.
\]

\[
  Q_s=\left(\frac{e^s+e^{-s}}{2},\frac{e^s-e^{-s}}{2}\right),
\]

$2\operatorname{HArea}(O,V,Q_s)=s$. Therefore the defining sector parameter is
$t=s$, and the displayed formulas follow. The negative case agrees with the
even/odd extension.

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Using the exponential form,
\[
  \cosh(a+b)

Expanding the right side of the claimed identity gives
\[

\]
The proof for $\sinh(a+b)$ is the same expansion with the signs arranged so
that the mixed exponential terms survive with the claimed signs.

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Let $t=\operatorname{arccosh}x$. Then $t\geq 0$ and
$x=\cosh t=(e^t+e^{-t})/2$. With $z=e^t\geq 1$, this becomes
$z^2-2xz+1=0$. The solution compatible with $z\geq 1$ is
$z=x+\sqrt{x^2-1}$, so $t=\log z$.

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Let $t=\operatorname{arctanh}x$. Then
\[
  x=\tanh t=\frac{e^t-e^{-t}}{e^t+e^{-t}}
  =\frac{e^{2t}-1}{e^{2t}+1}.
\]
Solving gives $e^{2t}=(1+x)/(1-x)$, whose right side is positive because
$-1<x<1$. Taking logarithms gives the formula.

stated domain, and taking logarithms gives the formula.

nodes.name: Inverse hyperbolic secant
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{inverse hyperbolic secant} function is the inverse of
$\operatorname{sech}$ after $\operatorname{sech}$ is restricted to
$[0,\infty)$. It is denoted by $\operatorname{arcsech}$ and has domain
$(0,1]$ and range $[0,\infty)$.
\[
  \operatorname{arcsech} x=t
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \operatorname{sech} t=x
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  t\geq 0.
\]

support_blocks.title: Proof
support_blocks.body_tex:
Parametrize the upper right branch by the $x$-coordinate:
\[
  P_x=(x,\sqrt{x^2-1}),\qquad x\geq 1.
\]
Let
\[
  F(x)=2\operatorname{HArea}(O,V,P_x).
\]
The sector area varies continuously with $x$: the boundary point depends
continuously on $x$, the function $\sqrt{x^2-1}$ is continuous on
$[1,\infty)$, and the area swept over a compact interval changes continuously
with the endpoint. Also $F(1)=0$, since the sector degenerates at $V$.
As $x\to\infty$, the swept sector area tends to infinity. Moreover, if
$1\leq x_1<x_2$, the sector from $V$ to $P_{x_1}$ is properly contained in
the sector from $V$ to $P_{x_2}$, so $F(x_1)<F(x_2)$. Thus $F$ is continuous,
strictly increasing, begins at $0$, and is unbounded. By the intermediate
value property, every $t\geq 0$ is equal to $F(x)$ for some $x\geq 1$.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $T_0$ and $T_1$ be theories. The theory $T_1$ is
\emph{consistent relative to $T_0$} if
\[
  \operatorname{Con}(T_0)\implies \operatorname{Con}(T_1).
\]
Equivalently, every contradiction in $T_1$ would imply a contradiction in
$T_0$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For theories $T_0$ and $T_1$,
\[
  \operatorname{RelCon}(T_1,T_0)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\neg\exists d_0\,(d_0:T_0\vdash\bot)\bigr)
  \implies
  \bigl(\neg\exists d_1\,(d_1:T_1\vdash\bot)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, in contrapositive form,
\[
  \exists d_1\,(d_1:T_1\vdash\bot)
  \implies
  \exists d_0\,(d_0:T_0\vdash\bot).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Relative consistency does not establish consistency from nothing. It says that
the target theory introduces no new contradiction unless the base theory was
already inconsistent. In practice, a relative consistency proof often gives a
translation that turns any contradiction derived in $T_1$ into a contradiction
derived in $T_0$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For every first-order signature $\mathcal{L}$, an $\mathcal{L}$-structure
consists of a nonempty domain $M$ and an interpretation $\mathcal{I}$ such
that every constant symbol is assigned an element of $M$, every $n$-ary
function symbol is assigned a function $M^n\to M$, and every $n$-ary relation
symbol is assigned a relation on $M^n$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A structure is the environment in which formal symbols receive meaning. The
domain supplies the objects, and the interpretation explains how the symbols
refer to objects, operations, and relations on that domain.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
In dependent type theory, this bundled data can be viewed schematically as
\[
\sum_{M:\mathrm{Type}}
\left(\prod_{c\in\mathcal{C}} M\right)
\times
\left(\prod_{f\in\mathcal{F}}(M^{\operatorname{ar}(f)}\to M)\right)
\times
\left(\prod_{R\in\mathcal{R}}(M^{\operatorname{ar}(R)}\to \mathrm{Prop})\right).
\]
This is the same semantic package represented by a Lean structure carrying a
carrier type, interpretations of constants and functions, and predicates for
relations.

nodes.name: Satisfaction
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\mathfrak{M}=(M,\mathcal{I})$ be an $\mathcal{L}$-structure. A
\emph{variable assignment} is a function $s:\operatorname{Var}\to M$. The
assignment extends recursively to a term-evaluation map $\bar{s}$ by
\[
  \bar{s}(x)=s(x),\qquad
  \bar{s}(c)=\mathcal{I}(c),
\]
and
\[
  \bar{s}\bigl(f(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\bigr)
  =
  \mathcal{I}(f)\bigl(\bar{s}(t_1),\ldots,\bar{s}(t_n)\bigr).
\]
The satisfaction relation $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi[s]$ is then defined by
induction on formulas: atomic relations are tested inside the interpreted
relation, equality is interpreted as equality in $M$, Boolean connectives are
interpreted by the corresponding truth operations, and quantifiers range over
all elements of $M$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
For terms $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ and an $n$-ary relation symbol $R$,
\[
  \mathfrak{M}\vDash R(t_1,\ldots,t_n)[s]
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\bar{s}(t_1),\ldots,\bar{s}(t_n)\bigr)\in\mathcal{I}(R).
\]
For equality,
\[
  \mathfrak{M}\vDash (t_1=t_2)[s]
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bar{s}(t_1)=\bar{s}(t_2).
\]
For quantifiers,
\[
  \mathfrak{M}\vDash(\forall x\,\varphi)[s]
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \forall a\in M,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi[s[x\mapsto a]],
\]
and
\[
  \mathfrak{M}\vDash(\exists x\,\varphi)[s]
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \exists a\in M,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi[s[x\mapsto a]].
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Satisfaction is the semantic test for a statement. Once the symbols have been
interpreted in a structure, the statement can be checked as true or false in

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
If $\varphi$ is a sentence, then it has no free variables, so its truth does
not depend on the initial assignment $s$. In that case the notation is
shortened from $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi[s]$ to $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi$.
This is the bridge from satisfaction of a single sentence to the definition of
a model of a theory.

nodes.name: Countermodel
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ be a set of premises,
let $\varphi\in\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$, and let $\mathfrak{M}$ be
an $\mathcal{L}$-structure. A \emph{countermodel to the entailment
$\Gamma\vDash\varphi$} is a structure $\mathfrak{M}$ that satisfies every
sentence in $\Gamma$ but does not satisfy $\varphi$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For $\Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$ and
$\varphi\in\operatorname{Sent}(\mathcal{L})$,
\[
  \mathfrak{M}\in\mathsf{CounterModel}(\Gamma,\varphi)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\forall \gamma\in\Gamma,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\not\vDash\varphi\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, for classical closed sentences,
\[
  \mathfrak{M}\in\mathsf{CounterModel}(\Gamma,\varphi)
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \bigl(\forall \gamma\in\Gamma,\; \mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma\bigr)
  \land
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\vDash\neg\varphi\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
The predicate form records the relation or property named by the statement in
the displayed logical context.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A countermodel shows that the theory does not force the statement. It keeps
the axioms true while making the proposed statement false.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
If $\Gamma=\emptyset$, then a countermodel to validity of $\varphi$ is a
structure $\mathfrak{M}$ such that $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\neg\varphi$. For a
theory $T$, models of $T$ satisfying $\varphi$ and models of $T$ satisfying
$\neg\varphi$ witness the independence pattern: the theory alone does not
settle $\varphi$.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
In a mechanized setting, invalidity is witnessed by constructing semantic
data:
\[
  \exists\mathfrak{M}\,
  \bigl((\forall\gamma\in\Gamma,\;\mathfrak{M}\vDash\gamma)
  \land
  \mathfrak{M}\vDash\neg\varphi\bigr).
\]
The constructed structure and satisfaction proofs are the certificate that the
entailment cannot be valid.

nodes.name: First-Order Signature
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{first-order signature} is a tuple
\[
  \Sigma=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar}),
\]
where $\mathcal{C}$ is a set of constant symbols, $\mathcal{F}$ is a set of
function symbols, $\mathcal{R}$ is a set of relation symbols, and
\[
  \operatorname{ar}:\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{R}\to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}
\]
assigns to each function or relation symbol its number of arguments.

Let $\Sigma=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar})$ be a
first-order signature. The \emph{arity function} is the map
\[

\]
that assigns to each function or relation symbol the number of arguments it
requires. When constants are treated as $0$-ary function symbols, the codomain
is enlarged to include $0$.

For every $s\in\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{R}$, there is a unique positive
integer $n$ such that $\operatorname{ar}(s)=n$. If $f\in\mathcal{F}$ and
$\operatorname{ar}(f)=n$, then an expression $f(t_1,\ldots,t_k)$ is a
well-formed term exactly when $k=n$. If $R\in\mathcal{R}$ and
$\operatorname{ar}(R)=n$, then an expression $R(t_1,\ldots,t_k)$ is a
well-formed atomic formula exactly when $k=n$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Arity is bookkeeping for grammatical well-formedness. It determines whether a
symbol has been supplied with the correct number of arguments.

nodes.name: Language
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{first-order language} has two standard readings. As vocabulary, it is
the same data as a signature,
\[
  \mathcal{L}=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{F},\mathcal{R},\operatorname{ar}).
\]
As a formal language generated by a signature $\Sigma$, it is the set of
well-formed strings built from the alphabet
\[
  A=\Sigma\cup V\cup\Lambda,
\]
where $V$ is a countable set of variables and $\Lambda$ is the fixed stock of
logical symbols and punctuation. In this second reading,
\[
  \mathcal{L}(\Sigma)
  =\{s\in A^* \mid s\in\operatorname{Terms}(\Sigma)
    \text{ or } s\in\operatorname{WFF}(\Sigma)\}.
\]

nodes.name: Constant Symbol
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{constant symbol} is a non-logical symbol that behaves syntactically as
a $0$-ary function symbol. In the streamlined convention where constants are
included among function symbols, this is the condition
\[
  c\in\mathsf{Constant}
  \iff c\in\mathcal{F}\text{ and }\operatorname{ar}(c)=0.
\]
Because its arity is $0$, the symbol $c$ is already a well-formed term and
takes no input terms.

A \emph{constant symbol} is a non-logical symbol that behaves syntactically as
a $0$-ary function symbol. In the streamlined convention where constants are
included among function symbols, this is the condition
\[
  c\in\mathsf{Constant}
  \iff c\in\mathcal{F}\text{ and }\operatorname{ar}(c)=0.
\]
Because its arity is $0$, the symbol $c$ is already a well-formed term and
takes no input terms.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A relation symbol is a statement-forming symbol once it is applied to the
right number of terms. In the arithmetic signature, $+$ is a binary function
symbol because it returns a number, while $<$ is a binary relation symbol
because it returns a truth value. Under the standard interpretation,
$<$ denotes the set of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ such that $a$ is less than $b$.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The same signature may support different choices of axioms later in the
chapter. For example, a single arithmetic vocabulary can be used with stronger
or weaker axiom sets.

The same signature may also be read over different mathematical universes once
interpretations are introduced. At this stage, the signature itself records
only the common vocabulary; it does not choose any particular interpretation.

nodes.name: Theory
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{theory} over a first-order language $\mathcal{L}$ is a collection of
closed sentences in that language:
\[
  T\subseteq\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L}).
\]
If $\Gamma$ is a chosen set of axioms, the theory generated by $\Gamma$ is the
deductive closure
\[
  T=\{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
      \Gamma\vdash\varphi\}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
Syntactically, a sentence $\varphi$ belongs to the theory generated by
$\Gamma$ exactly when $\varphi$ is derivable from $\Gamma$. Semantically, for
an $\mathcal{L}$-structure $\mathfrak{M}$, the complete theory of
$\mathfrak{M}$ is
\[
  \operatorname{Th}(\mathfrak{M})
  =\{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
      \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi\}.
\]
For every sentence $\varphi$, either $\mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi$ or
$\mathfrak{M}\vDash\neg\varphi$, so $\operatorname{Th}(\mathfrak{M})$
decides every sentence of the language.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A theory is not merely the list of axioms. It is the closure of those axioms
under derivability: every statement that follows from the axioms belongs to
the theory. The axioms start the system; the theory records everything the
system proves.

nodes.name: Theorem
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{theorem} of a theory $T$ is a sentence $\varphi$ for which there is a
finite formal derivation from $T$, written
\[
  T\vdash\varphi.
\]
Equivalently, in proof-theoretic terms, $\varphi$ is a theorem of $T$ exactly
when some derivation has leaves drawn from logical axioms or sentences of
$T$, uses valid inference rules, and has $\varphi$ as its root.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
Syntactically,
\[
  \varphi\in\mathsf{Theorem}(T)
  \iff \exists d\ (d:T\vdash\varphi).
\]
Semantically, $\varphi$ is entailed by $T$ when it is true in every model of
$T$:
\[
  T\vDash\varphi
  \iff
  \forall\mathfrak{M}\,
  \bigl(\mathfrak{M}\vDash T \implies \mathfrak{M}\vDash\varphi\bigr).
\]
For first-order logic, the completeness theorem connects these readings:
$T\vdash\varphi$ exactly when $T\vDash\varphi$.

of $\Gamma$ are true while $\varphi$ is false.

\[
  \Gamma\vDash\varphi
  \iff

  \Bigl(

\]
Syntactic consequence, written $\Gamma\vdash\varphi$, means that there exists
a finite valid deduction of $\varphi$ from $\Gamma$. For first-order logic,
the completeness theorem says that $\Gamma\vDash\varphi$ exactly when
$\Gamma\vdash\varphi$.

$\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma)$, is the set of all sentences derivable from

\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
A set of sentences $T$ is deductively closed exactly when
\[
  T=\operatorname{Cn}(T),
\]
or equivalently, for every sentence $\varphi$,
\[
  T\vdash\varphi \implies \varphi\in T.
\]
The closure operator satisfies the standard Tarskian closure laws:
\[
  \Gamma\subseteq\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma),
  \qquad
  \Gamma\subseteq\Delta\implies
  \operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma)\subseteq\operatorname{Cn}(\Delta),
  \qquad
  \operatorname{Cn}(\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma))
  =\operatorname{Cn}(\Gamma).
\]
By completeness for first-order logic, this syntactic closure agrees with the
semantic closure
\[
  \{\varphi\in\operatorname{Sentences}(\mathcal{L})\mid
    \Gamma\vDash\varphi\}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Deductive closure is the operation that turns an axiom system into the full
theory it generates. Starting with the axioms, close under derivability; the
result is the theory determined by those starting assertions.

contradiction), then $\Gamma$ has a model.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Soundness ensures proofs do not lead from true premises to false conclusions.
Completeness ensures proofs are powerful enough: every statement that is true
in all models can be established by a formal proof.

Together, soundness and completeness show that syntactic provability ($\vdash$)
and semantic entailment ($\models$) coincide for first-order logic.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
G\"{o}del's completeness theorem (1930) should not be confused with his
incompleteness theorems (1931). The completeness theorem concerns first-order
logic as a proof system. The incompleteness theorems concern the limitations of
formal theories capable of expressing arithmetic, and are a separate result.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The dependent-witness statement allows \(y\) to vary with \(x\). The uniform
statement requires one \(y\) to handle all \(x\) at once.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Over \(\mathbb R\), let \(\varphi(x,y)\) be \(y>x\). Then
\(\forall x\,\exists y\,(y>x)\) is true, since \(y=x+1\) works for each \(x\).
But \(\exists y\,\forall x\,(y>x)\) is false, since no real number is larger
than every real number.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Quantifier order matters because it records dependency. The phrase "for every
\(x\), there exists \(y\)" permits a different \(y\) after \(x\) is known. The
phrase "there exists \(y\) such that for every \(x\)" chooses \(y\) before
seeing \(x\). This is a genuine expressive jump beyond propositional logic.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Prenex normal form is not unique. Different choices of bound-variable names and
different orders of valid pulling steps can produce different but logically
equivalent prenex formulas.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
A prenex conversion proceeds in stages: eliminate implications and
biconditionals, push negations inward, rename bound variables as needed, pull
quantifiers forward, and leave a quantifier-free matrix.

forward to obtain

\]

nodes.text_preview: Let \(\varphi\) be a sentence and let \(\mathcal M\) be a structure for the language of \(\varphi\). The structure \(\mathcal M\) is a \emph{model of} \(\varphi\) exactly when \(\mathcal M\models\varphi\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\mathcal M \text{ is a model of } \varphi
\Longleftrightarrow
\mathcal M\models\varphi.
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\operatorname{ModelOfSentence}(M,\varphi)\) means that \(M\) is a model of
the sentence \(\varphi\).

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\mathcal M \text{ is not a model of } \varphi
\Longleftrightarrow
\mathcal M\not\models\varphi.
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\neg\operatorname{ModelOfSentence}(M,\varphi)\) means that \(\varphi\) is not
true in \(M\).

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
The only failure mode is semantic: the sentence is false in the proposed
structure.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[
\underbrace{\mathcal M}_{\text{proposed structure}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\mathcal M\not\models\varphi}_{\text{sentence false in the structure}}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A model is not an extra kind of object. It is a structure viewed relative to a
sentence that it makes true.

nodes.name: Model of a Set of Sentences
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(T\) be a set of sentences and let \(\mathcal M\) be a structure for their
common language. The structure \(\mathcal M\) is a \emph{model of} \(T\),
written \(\mathcal M\models T\), exactly when
\(\mathcal M\models\theta\) for every \(\theta\in T\).

nodes.name: Theory
nodes.statement_display:
In Volume I, a \emph{theory} is a set of sentences in a fixed first-order
language.
nodes.statement_tex:

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
T \text{ is a theory}
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall \theta\in T\;(\theta \text{ is a sentence of the fixed language}).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(T\in\mathsf{Theory}\) means that \(T\) is a set of sentences in a fixed
first-order language.

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\exists \theta\in T\;(\theta \text{ is not a sentence of the fixed language}).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(T\notin\mathsf{Theory}\) means that \(T\) is not a set consisting only
of sentences of the fixed language.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
A proposed theory fails in this minimal sense when it contains something other
than a sentence of the fixed language.

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[

\qquad

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is intentionally modest. Complete theories, elementary classes,
categoricity, saturation, types, diagrams, and elementary extensions are
Volume VIII topics. A theory may be called satisfiable in Volume I when it has
at least one model.

nodes.name: Logical Consequence
nodes.statement_display:

language. The sentence \(\varphi\) is a \emph{logical consequence} of \(T\),
written \(T\models\varphi\), exactly when every model of \(T\) is a model of
\(\varphi\).

nodes.name: Logical Equivalence
nodes.statement_display:
Two sentences \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are \emph{logically equivalent}, written
\(\varphi\equiv\psi\), exactly when each is a logical consequence of the other:
\[
\varphi\models\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\models\varphi.
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\varphi\equiv\psi
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall \mathcal M\;(\mathcal M\models\varphi \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal M\models\psi).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\operatorname{LogicalEquivalence}(\varphi,\psi)\) means that \(\varphi\) and
\(\psi\) have the same truth value in every structure.

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\varphi\not\equiv\psi
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists \mathcal M\;\bigl((\mathcal M\models\varphi \land \mathcal M\not\models\psi)
\lor
(\mathcal M\models\psi \land \mathcal M\not\models\varphi)\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\neg\operatorname{LogicalEquivalence}(\varphi,\psi)\) means that some
structure separates the two sentences.

nodes.name: Open Formula
nodes.statement_display:
An \emph{open formula} is a well-formed formula with at least one free
variable. When the free variables are among \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), it may be
displayed as \(\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Open formulas are syntactic predicates in the lightest Volume I sense. They do
not by themselves name a set-theoretic relation until a structure is fixed.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(P(x)\), \(x<y\), and \(\exists z\,R(x,z)\) are open formulas when the
displayed variables remain free as indicated.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\forall x\,P(x)\) is a sentence, not an open formula. A predicate symbol
\(P\) alone is a symbol, not a formula.

nodes.name: Definable Relation
nodes.statement_display:

\(\varphi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be an open formula. The \emph{relation defined by}
\(\varphi\) in \(\mathcal M\) is the set
\[
R_{\varphi}^{\mathcal M}
=
\{(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in D^n:
\mathcal M,s[x_1\mapsto a_1,\ldots,x_n\mapsto a_n]\models\varphi\}.
\]

assignment, and let \(\varphi\) be a well-formed formula. The relation

conditions for \(\neg,\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\); and

\]

modes.body_tex:
Satisfaction fails according to the outermost formation rule of the formula:
an atomic tuple can miss the interpreted relation, equality can compare
different term values, a connective can have the wrong truth pattern, or a
quantifier can have a counterexample or lack a witness.

\underbrace{\exists d\in D\;(\mathcal M,s[x\mapsto d]\not\models\psi)}_{\text{universal failure}}.
\]

symbols, and a signature of non-logical symbols: constant symbols, function
symbols with assigned arities, and predicate symbols with assigned arities.
Equality may be included as a distinguished logical predicate.

support_blocks.body_tex:
A first-order language is still syntax. It says which expressions can be
formed, but it does not assign objects, functions, or relations to the
non-logical symbols.

\(\mathcal L\) is a pair

of \(D\), each \(n\)-ary function symbol a function \(D^n\to D\), and each
\(n\)-ary predicate symbol a relation on \(D^n\).

nodes.name: Formula Depth
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{depth} (or \emph{complexity}) of a formula $\varphi$, denoted
$\mathrm{depth}(\varphi)$, is a natural number defined recursively:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Atomic case.} If $\varphi$ is atomic, then $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = 0$.

  \item \textbf{Negation.} If $\varphi = \neg \psi$, then
  $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \mathrm{depth}(\psi) + 1$.

  \item \textbf{Binary connectives.} If $\varphi = (\psi \circ \chi)$
  for $\circ \in \{\wedge,\vee,\rightarrow,\leftrightarrow\}$, then
  \[
  \mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \max\{\mathrm{depth}(\psi),\,\mathrm{depth}(\chi)\} + 1.
  \]

  \item \textbf{Quantifiers.} If $\varphi = \forall x\,\psi$ or $\varphi = \exists x\,\psi$,
  then $\mathrm{depth}(\varphi) = \mathrm{depth}(\psi) + 1$.
\end{enumerate}

non-logical symbol of arity \(0\). A constant symbol may occur as a term without
taking input terms.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A constant symbol is a simple name-forming symbol in the grammar. It supplies a
base case for terms alongside variables.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
In an arithmetic language, \(0\) and \(1\) are commonly used as constant
symbols.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(f(x)\) is not a constant symbol; it is a term built from a function symbol
and an input term.

non-logical symbol of \(\mathcal L\).

nodes.name: Function Symbol
nodes.statement_display:
For a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), an \(n\)-ary \emph{function symbol}
is a non-logical symbol of arity \(n\geq 1\). If \(f\) has arity \(n\), then it
forms terms by the pattern
\[
f(t_1,\ldots,t_n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A function symbol is an operation-forming symbol in the grammar. It is not a
term by itself; it becomes part of a term only after it is supplied the required
number of input terms.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
In an arithmetic language, \(S\) may be unary, while \(+\) and \(\cdot\) may be
binary function symbols.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(f(x)\) is not a function symbol. It is a term formed by applying the function
symbol \(f\) to the term \(x\).

function symbol of \(\mathcal L\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Predicate symbols are the atomic-formula-forming vocabulary of the language.
They are syntactic symbols, not project metalanguage predicates.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(P\), \(Q\), \(R\), \(<\), and \(=\) may be predicate symbols when the language
declares the corresponding arities.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(P(x)\) is not a predicate symbol. It is an atomic formula formed from the
predicate symbol \(P\) and the term \(x\).

nodes.text_preview: The set of \emph{terms} of a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), denoted \(\mathsf{Term}_{\mathcal L}\), is the smallest set of strings satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item every variable is a term; \item every constant symbol is a term; \i

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex: \(t\in\mathsf{Term}\) means \(t\in\mathsf{Term}_{\mathcal L}\).

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\sigma\notin\mathsf{Term}_{\mathcal L}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists S
\left[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathsf{Var}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq S
\land
\mathsf{Const}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq S\\
&\land
(\forall n\geq 1)(\forall f\in\mathsf{Func}_{\mathcal L}^{(n)})
(\forall t_1,\ldots,t_n\in S)
f(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\in S\\
&\land\ \sigma\notin S
\end{aligned}
\right].
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\sigma\notin\mathsf{Term}\) means that \(\sigma\) is not generated by
the term-formation clauses.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
A string fails to be a term when it uses a predicate symbol, connective, or
quantifier at the outer syntactic level, when a function symbol has too few or
too many input terms, or when punctuation does not match the arity pattern.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[
\underbrace{P(x)}_{\text{atomic formula, not a term}}
\qquad
\underbrace{f(x,y)}_{\text{wrong arity if }f\text{ is unary}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\forall x}_{\text{quantifier fragment}}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Terms are the noun-like expressions of first-order syntax. They provide the
inputs to predicate symbols but do not themselves make assertions.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(x\), \(c\), \(f(x)\), \(g(c,x)\), and \(h(f(x),c)\) are terms when the
language assigns the displayed arities.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex: \(P(x)\), \(\neg P(x)\), \(\forall x\,P(x)\), and \(x\land y\) are not terms.

nodes.name: Atomic Formula
nodes.statement_display:
An \emph{atomic formula} of a first-order language \(\mathcal L\) is a string
of the form
\[
P(t_1,\ldots,t_n),
\]
where \(P\) is an \(n\)-ary predicate symbol and
\(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) are terms.

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
A string fails to be atomic when it does not begin with a predicate symbol,
when the predicate symbol receives the wrong number of term inputs, when an
input is not a term, or when a logical connective or quantifier has already
been applied.

\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Atomic formulas are the base cases of formula formation. They are the first
strings in the grammar that count as formulas.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(P(x)\), \(R(x,c)\), \(x=y\), and \(x<y\) are atomic formulas when the
language supplies the relevant predicate symbols and arities.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(x\), \(f(x)\), \(\neg P(x)\), and \((P(x)\land Q(x))\) are not atomic
formulas.

nodes.name: Formula
nodes.statement_display:
For a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), a \emph{formula} is an expression
formed by the formula grammar of \(\mathcal L\). The grammar starts from atomic
formulas and closes under the logical connectives and quantifiers of the
language.

nodes.name: Well-Formed Formula
nodes.text_preview: The set of \emph{well-formed formulas} of a first-order language \(\mathcal L\), denoted \(\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}\), is the smallest set of strings satisfying: \begin{enumerate} \item every atomic formula is a well-formed formula; \item

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}
=
\bigcap\{S:\;&
\mathsf{Atom}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq S,\\
&(\forall\varphi\in S)(\neg\varphi\in S),\\
&(\forall\varphi,\psi\in S)
(\forall\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\})
((\varphi\circ\psi)\in S),\\
&(\forall x\in\mathsf{Var}_{\mathcal L})(\forall\varphi\in S)
(\forall x\,\varphi\in S\land \exists x\,\varphi\in S)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\varphi\in\mathsf{WellFormedFormula}\) means
\(\varphi\in\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}\).

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\varphi\notin\mathsf{Form}_{\mathcal L}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists S\left[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathsf{Atom}_{\mathcal L}\subseteq S
\land
(\forall\psi\in S)(\neg\psi\in S)\\
&\land
(\forall\psi,\chi\in S)
(\forall\circ\in\{\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\})
((\psi\circ\chi)\in S)\\
&\land
(\forall x\in\mathsf{Var}_{\mathcal L})(\forall\psi\in S)
(\forall x\,\psi\in S\land \exists x\,\psi\in S)\\
&\land\ \varphi\notin S
\end{aligned}
\right].
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\varphi\notin\mathsf{WellFormedFormula}\) means that \(\varphi\) is not
generated by the formula-formation clauses.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
A string fails to be well formed when it is a bare term, has a missing operand,
uses a quantifier without a variable and formula, has unmatched punctuation, or
cannot be produced by finitely many formation steps.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:

\(\forall x\,(P(x)\to Q(x))\) are well-formed formulas.

nodes.name: Molecular Formula
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{molecular formula} is a well-formed formula that is not atomic.
Equivalently, it is a well-formed formula whose final formation step uses a
logical connective or a quantifier.

nodes.name: Scope of a Quantifier
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\varphi$ be a formula of a first-order language.

If $\varphi$ is of the form $\forall x\,\psi$ or $\exists x\,\psi$, then the
formula $\psi$ is called the \emph{scope} of the quantifier.

The quantifier is said to \emph{bind} all occurrences of the variable $x$ that
appear within its scope.

support_blocks.body_tex:
For every admissible object satisfying the hypotheses of the statement, the
assertion holds in the formal language under discussion.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The statement records the named logical notion or result together with its
intended syntactic or semantic role.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The scope is the reach of a quantifier --- the subformula it governs. Scope is
syntactically determined by the parenthesisation of the formula, not by
proximity to the quantifier symbol.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
In $(\forall x\,P(x)) \wedge Q(x)$, the scope of $\forall x$ is $P(x)$ only.
The occurrence of $x$ in $Q(x)$ falls outside the scope and is free.

nodes.statement_display:

lies within the scope of a quantifier $\forall x$ or $\exists x$.

An occurrence of $x$ is \emph{free} if it is not bound by any quantifier in
$\varphi$.

nodes.name: Free Variables of a Formula
nodes.statement_display:
The set $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$ of \emph{free variables} of a formula $\varphi$
is defined recursively:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item If $\varphi = P(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ is atomic, then
  $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi) = \bigcup_{i=1}^n \mathrm{Var}(t_i)$,
  where $\mathrm{Var}(t_i)$ is the set of variables in term $t_i$.

  \item $\mathrm{FV}(\neg \varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi)$.

  \item $\mathrm{FV}(\varphi \circ \psi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \cup \mathrm{FV}(\psi)$
  for any binary connective $\circ$.

  \item $\mathrm{FV}(\forall x\,\varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}$.

  \item $\mathrm{FV}(\exists x\,\varphi) = \mathrm{FV}(\varphi) \setminus \{x\}$.
\end{enumerate}

The expression $\varphi[t/x]$ denotes the formula obtained from $\varphi$ by
replacing every \emph{free} occurrence of $x$ with the term $t$, leaving bound
occurrences of $x$ unchanged.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
The relation ``$t$ is free for $x$ in $\varphi$'' is defined by structural
induction on formulas. It is automatic for atomic formulas. It is preserved
through Boolean connectives:
\[
  t\text{ free for }x\text{ in }\neg\varphi
  \iff
  t\text{ free for }x\text{ in }\varphi,
\]
and similarly componentwise for $\varphi\land\psi$, $\varphi\lor\psi$, and
$\varphi\to\psi$. For a quantified formula, the capture-avoidance condition is
\[
  t\text{ free for }x\text{ in }Qy\,\varphi
  \iff
  \bigl(x\text{ is not free in }Qy\,\varphi\bigr)
  \text{ or }
  \bigl(y\notin\operatorname{Var}(t)
    \text{ and }t\text{ is free for }x\text{ in }\varphi\bigr),
\]
where $Q$ is either $\forall$ or $\exists$.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
The predicate form records the relation or property named by the statement in
the displayed logical context.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The statement records the named logical notion or result together with its
intended syntactic or semantic role.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
A substitution $\varphi[t/x]$ is admissible only if $t$ is free for $x$ in
$\varphi$. If this condition is violated, a variable occurring in $t$ may
become bound after substitution, silently changing the meaning of the formula.
This is called \emph{variable capture}.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Variable capture is one of the most common syntactic mistakes in predicate
logic. Always check that the term being substituted introduces no variables that
fall inside a binding quantifier in the target formula.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
In the formula $\exists y\,(x<y)$, the term $y+1$ is not free for $x$. A blind
substitution would produce $\exists y\,(y+1<y)$, where the $y$ introduced by
the term has been captured by the existing quantifier.

nodes.name: Translation Key
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{translation key} is a finite record that fixes a domain of discourse and
assigns intended English readings to the constant symbols, predicate symbols,
and relation symbols used in a translation.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(K\in\mathsf{TranslationKey}\) means that \(K\) supplies the domain and
symbol readings needed to parse a translated formula.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A translation key prevents hidden changes of meaning. The same symbol must keep
the same reading throughout one exercise unless the key is explicitly replaced.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
For the English sentence ``Every applicant submitted some form,'' a key may
take the domain to be people and forms, with \(A(x)\) for ``\(x\) is an
applicant,'' \(F(y)\) for ``\(y\) is a form,'' and \(S(x,y)\) for ``\(x\)
submitted \(y\).''

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
Using \(P(x)\) once for ``\(x\) is a person'' and later for ``\(x\) passed'' is
not a translation key; it is a change of vocabulary inside one translation.

support_blocks.body_tex:
The domain decides what the quantifiers are allowed to talk about. If the
domain is people, then an exam must either be named by a separate sort-like
predicate or represented by a different translation choice.

For ``All cats are mammals,'' one may use the domain of all animals and write
\(\forall x\,(C(x)\to M(x))\). With the smaller domain of cats, the same English
claim may be written \(\forall x\,M(x)\).

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
Writing \(\forall x\,M(x)\) while silently changing the domain from animals to
cats halfway through the exercise is not a valid translation.

nodes.statement_display:
In a translation key, a unary predicate symbol names a property of one object,
and an \(n\)-ary relation symbol names a relation among \(n\) objects.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(P\in\mathsf{TranslationPredicateSymbol}(K)\) records that \(P\) has a
fixed predicate reading in \(K\), and \(R\in\mathsf{TranslationRelationSymbol}(n,K)\)
records that \(R\) is used with arity \(n\) in \(K\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Object-language predicate symbols such as \(P,Q,R\) are symbols inside the
formal language. Metalinguistic predicate readings such as
\(t\in\mathsf{Term}\) or \(\varphi\in\mathsf{AtomicFormula}\) are
repository descriptions of syntax; they are not formulas being translated.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(A(x)\) may mean ``\(x\) is an athlete.'' \(L(x,y)\) may mean ``\(x\) likes
\(y\).'' The arity is part of the key: \(L(x)\) and \(L(x,y)\) are not the same
symbol use.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
Writing \(L(x,y,z)\) after declaring \(L(x,y)\) as ``\(x\) likes \(y\)'' is an
arity error.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(c\in\mathsf{TranslationConstant}(K)\) means that \(c\) names a fixed
object in \(K\), and \(x\in\mathsf{TranslationVariable}(K)\) means that
\(x\) is used as a variable in translations governed by \(K\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Constants do not range. Variables do range when bound by quantifiers. Confusing
the two usually leaves a formula with the wrong dependency pattern.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
If \(a\) names Alice, then \(P(a)\) says Alice is a participant. The formula
\(\forall x\,(S(x)\to P(x))\) uses \(x\) as a bound variable.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
The expression \(\forall a\,S(a)\) is not appropriate if \(a\) has already been
declared as a constant naming Alice.

nodes.name: Universal Translation Pattern
nodes.statement_display:
In a broad domain, an English statement of the form ``All \(A\) are \(B\)''
is translated by
\[
\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x)).
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x)).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\((A,B)\in\mathsf{UniversalTranslationPattern}\) records the implication
schema for translating universal restricted claims.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The antecedent \(A(x)\) restricts attention to the relevant objects. Objects
outside \(A\) do not have to satisfy \(B\).

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
``All cats are mammals'' becomes \(\forall x\,(C(x)\to M(x))\). ``No cats are
reptiles'' becomes \(\forall x\,(C(x)\to \neg R(x))\). The form
\(\forall x\,(C(x)\land M(x))\) says every object in the domain is both a cat
and a mammal, which is far stronger than the intended restricted claim. In a
broad domain, ``all,'' ``every,'' and ``any'' usually translate restricted
claims with implication.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x)).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\((A,B)\in\mathsf{ExistentialTranslationPattern}\) records the conjunction
schema for translating existential restricted claims.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The witness must satisfy both restrictions at once. Existence is not merely a
conditional promise about what would happen if an \(A\) existed.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
``Some cats are black'' becomes \(\exists x\,(C(x)\land B(x))\). ``Some cats are
not black'' becomes \(\exists x\,(C(x)\land \neg B(x))\). The form
\(\exists x\,(C(x)\to B(x))\) may be true because the witness is not a cat, so
it does not translate ``Some cats are black.'' In a broad domain, ``some,''
``there is,'' and ``at least one'' usually translate restricted claims with
conjunction.

support_blocks.body_tex:

support_blocks.body_tex:
Conditionals are especially common inside universal translations. The
conditional separates the restricting condition from the asserted consequence.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
``Every applicant who is eligible is interviewed'' becomes

\(\forall x\,(A(x)\land E(x)\land I(x))\) says every object is an eligible
applicant who is interviewed, which is not the intended conditional claim.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\((\varphi,\psi)\in\mathsf{NegationTranslationPattern}\) records that
\(\psi\) is obtained from \(\neg\varphi\) by pushing negation through the
quantifiers and connectives.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The negation of ``all'' is ``some not.'' The negation of ``some'' is ``none.''
For restricted universal claims, negating the implication produces a witness
that satisfies the restriction and fails the consequent.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The negation of \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))\) is
\(\exists x\,(A(x)\land \neg B(x))\). The negation of
\(\exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x))\) is \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to \neg B(x))\). The
negation of \(\forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))\) is not
\(\forall x\,(A(x)\to \neg B(x))\); that latter formula says every \(A\) fails
to be \(B\), not merely that some counterexample exists.

nodes.name: Scope Ambiguity
nodes.statement_display:
A sentence has \emph{scope ambiguity} when the same ordinary-language wording
admits two or more translations with different quantifier nesting or different
connective scope.
nodes.statement_tex:
A sentence has \emph{scope ambiguity} when the same ordinary-language wording

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\operatorname{ScopeAmbiguity}(E,\varphi,\psi)\) means that the English
sentence \(E\) can reasonably be translated by \(\varphi\) or by \(\psi\), and
the difference is a scope difference.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Scope is not cosmetic. Changing the outer quantifier can change whether a
single witness works for everyone or whether each object may have its own
witness.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formulas \(\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)\) and
\(\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)\) are not interchangeable. The first allows the
witness \(y\) to depend on \(x\); the second requires one \(y\) that works for
every \(x\). Symbols such as \(A(x)\), \(B(x)\), and \(R(x,y)\) are
object-language formula patterns used in translations. Expressions such as
\(K\in\mathsf{TranslationKey}\), \(t\in\mathsf{Term}\), and
\(\varphi\in\mathsf{AtomicFormula}\) are metalinguistic predicate readings
used by the project to describe mathematical objects.
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
\text{All }A\text{ are }B
  &\leadsto& \forall x\,(A(x)\to B(x))\\
\text{Some }A\text{ are }B
  &\leadsto& \exists x\,(A(x)\land B(x))\\
\text{No }A\text{ are }B
  &\leadsto& \forall x\,(A(x)\to \neg B(x))\\
\text{Some }A\text{ are not }B
  &\leadsto& \exists x\,(A(x)\land \neg B(x))\\
\text{Every }A\text{ has a }B
  &\leadsto& \forall x\,(A(x)\to \exists y\,(B(y)\land R(x,y)))\\
\text{There is a }B\text{ for every }A
  &\leadsto& \exists y\,(B(y)\land \forall x\,(A(x)\to R(x,y))).
\end{array}
\]

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
``Every \(A\) has a \(B\)'' is usually
\(\forall x\,(A(x)\to \exists y\,(B(y)\land R(x,y)))\). ``There is a \(B\) for
every \(A\)'' is usually
\(\exists y\,(B(y)\land \forall x\,(A(x)\to R(x,y)))\). The bare patterns
\(\forall x\exists y\,R(x,y)\) and \(\exists y\forall x\,R(x,y)\) make the same
scope contrast visible.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
Renaming a bound variable from \(x\) to \(z\) does not create a scope ambiguity.
The scope is unchanged.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:

\(\neg B\) of that object. Without such an object, both universals may be
vacuously true. The traditional square of opposition assumes existential
import; modern first-order logic does not automatically assume that a universal
statement implies existence.

nodes.name: Basic Boolean Equivalence Laws
nodes.statement_display:
For all formulas \(\varphi,\psi,\chi\in\WFF\), the following logical equivalences hold.

Commutativity:
\[
\varphi\land\psi\equiv\psi\land\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv\psi\lor\varphi.
\]

Associativity:
\[
(\varphi\land\psi)\land\chi
\equiv
\varphi\land(\psi\land\chi),
\qquad
(\varphi\lor\psi)\lor\chi
\equiv
\varphi\lor(\psi\lor\chi).
\]

Idempotence:
\[
\varphi\land\varphi\equiv\varphi,
\qquad
\varphi\lor\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]

Double negation:
\[
\neg\neg\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Logical equivalence is substitutive: equivalent formulas may be replaced inside larger formulas without changing truth behavior.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The equivalence laws in this section may be used as replacement rules inside
larger formulas. If a formula contains a subformula matching one side of a listed
equivalence law, that subformula may be replaced by the other side.

Common replacement rules include:
\[
\neg\neg\varphi \equiv \varphi,
\]
\[
\neg(\varphi\land\psi)\equiv \neg\varphi\lor\neg\psi,
\qquad
\neg(\varphi\lor\psi)\equiv \neg\varphi\land\neg\psi,
\]
\[
\varphi\to\psi\equiv \neg\varphi\lor\psi,
\]
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi),
\]
and
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\land\psi)\lor(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi).
\]

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex: The laws in this section allow formulas to be manipulated algebraically. They are not new formation rules; they are semantic equivalences. Later sections use these laws to transform formulas into normal forms and to reduce the set of primitive connectives.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex: The algebra of propositions is the bridge from semantics to computation: once formulas are equivalent, they can be rewritten without changing truth behavior.

conclusion under the same truth assignment.

nodes.name: Informal Proof Pattern
nodes.statement_display:
An \emph{informal proof pattern} is a reusable truth-preserving strategy for
organizing an ordinary mathematical proof.
nodes.statement_tex:

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\Pi\in\mathsf{InformalProofPattern}\) means that \(\Pi\) is a recognized
proof strategy whose correctness rests on truth-preserving inference.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Informal proof patterns are not a substitute for proof. They are templates for
arranging valid moves so that a proof has a clear logical shape.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
A direct proof establishes a target conclusion by moving forward from known
premises through valid argument forms. A conditional proof establishes
\(\varphi\to\psi\) by assuming \(\varphi\) and deriving \(\psi\) inside that
assumption context. Proof by cases uses a disjunction of cases and shows that
each case leads to the desired conclusion.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Proof by contradiction assumes the negation of the desired conclusion and derives
an impossible situation. Contrapositive proof establishes \(\varphi\to\psi\) by
showing \(\neg\psi\to\neg\varphi\). Chain-of-implications proofs use repeated
hypothetical syllogism, while equivalence-chain proofs use replacement and
logical equivalence.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
If the target has the form \(\varphi\to\psi\), a conditional proof is often
natural. If the available information has the form \(\varphi\lor\psi\), proof by
cases is often natural. If the target is an equivalence, an equivalence chain or
two conditional proofs are often natural.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
A finite sequence of equivalence-preserving replacements preserves logical
equivalence from the first formula to the last formula.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Replacement rules justify algebraic manipulation of formulas. Each local rewrite
preserves truth under every truth assignment, so the entire finite rewrite chain
also preserves truth under every truth assignment.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Common replacement rules include double negation, De Morgan replacement,
commutativity, associativity, distributivity, material implication, biconditional
replacement, and contraposition. Each is justified by a logical equivalence law.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
If the conditional from the conjunction of all premises to the conclusion is
always true, then the premises cannot all be true while the conclusion is false.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem converts a tautology check into an argument-validity check. It is
one reason truth tables can validate named inference rules.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The semantic proof pattern for a valid argument form is always the same. Let an
arbitrary truth assignment make all premises true. Then show that the conclusion
must also be true. If this can be done for an arbitrary truth assignment, then no
counterexample assignment exists.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
This section does not yet define formal derivations. The word valid here is
semantic: it refers to preservation of truth under truth assignments. Later proof
systems will turn selected valid patterns into formal rules of inference.

\]

nodes.name: Expressively Equivalent Connective Sets

connective in \(B\) is definable from \(C\), and every connective in \(C\) is
definable from \(B\).

changing input coordinates from \(\False\) to \(\True\) never changes the output
from \(\True\) to \(\False\).

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{Monotone}(f)
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a,b\in\mathbb{B}^n)
\bigl(a\le b\to f(a)\le f(b)\bigr),
\]
where \(\False\le\True\) coordinatewise.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\operatorname{Monotone}(f)\) means that increasing truth inputs cannot make the
output decrease from true to false.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The connectives \(\land\) and \(\lor\) are monotone. Negation is not monotone,
because changing \(P\) from false to true changes \(\neg P\) from true to false.

support_blocks.body_tex:
There is at least one Boolean function that cannot be represented by any formula

support_blocks.body_tex:

Boolean function. Since negation is not monotone, no formula using only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) can represent negation. Hence the basis is incomplete.

\[
\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(B)
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{FunctionallyComplete}(B)
\land

support_blocks.body_tex:
\(\operatorname{MinimalComplete}(B)\) means that \(B\) is complete, but removing
any primitive connective from \(B\) destroys completeness.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation

mean that formulas using the basis are short or easy to read.

\(\varphi\) and \(\psi\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation

nodes.name: Connective Reduction
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{connective reduction} replaces a formula using one connective basis by
a logically equivalent formula using a smaller or different connective basis.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
(\varphi,\psi)\in\mathsf{Reduction}_{B\to C}
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi\equiv\psi
\quad\text{and}\quad
\psi\in\WFF_C.
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\((\varphi,\psi)\in\mathsf{Reduction}_{B\to C}\) means that \(\psi\) is a
translation of \(\varphi\) into the connective basis \(C\) without changing truth
behavior.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Reduction shows that some primitive connectives are optional. If a connective is
definable from the remaining basis, then formulas using that connective can be
translated away.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The standard reductions are:
\[
\varphi\to\psi\equiv\neg\varphi\lor\psi,
\]
\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\varphi\to\psi)\land(\psi\to\varphi),
\]
\[
\varphi\lor\psi\equiv\neg(\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi),
\qquad
\varphi\land\psi\equiv\neg(\neg\varphi\lor\neg\psi).
\]
Each replacement preserves logical equivalence and may be performed inside a
larger formula context.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Reducing a connective basis can make formulas longer. Functional completeness is
therefore an expressive result, not an efficiency result. A small basis may be
powerful enough to express every Boolean function while still being awkward for
ordinary human-readable formulas.

\hyperref[def:truth-table-propositional-logic]{truth table} for those
variables. The \emph{truth-table row conjunction} for \(r\) is the conjunction
\[

\]
where
\[

P_i, & \text{if row }r\text{ makes }P_i\text{ true},\\
\neg P_i, & \text{if row }r\text{ makes }P_i\text{ false}.
\end{cases}
\]

\]
where each \(L_i\) is a literal. The one-literal case is permitted.

nodes.name: Conjunctive Normal Form
nodes.statement_display:
A formula is in \emph{conjunctive normal form}, abbreviated \emph{CNF}, when it
is a finite conjunction of
\hyperref[def:clause-propositional-logic]{clauses}. Equivalently, it has the
shape
\[
C_1\land C_2\land\cdots\land C_m,
\]
where each \(C_j\) is a clause.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\varphi\text{ is in CNF}
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi=C_1\land C_2\land\cdots\land C_m
\]
for finitely many clauses \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
CNF is a syntactic form used to expose clause-by-clause constraints. Replacing
a formula by a
\hyperref[def:logical-equivalence-propositional-logic]{logically equivalent}
CNF formula turns global validity and
\hyperref[def:contradiction-propositional-logic]{contradiction} questions into
questions about the interaction of its clauses.

nodes.name: Elementary Conjunction

\hyperref[def:literal-propositional-logic]{literals}. That is, it is a
\hyperref[def:term-propositional-logic]{term} of the form

\]
where each \(L_i\) is a literal. The one-literal case is permitted.

nodes.name: Literal
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{literal} is either a propositional variable \(P\) or the negation
\(\neg P\) of a propositional variable \(P\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For a formula \(\ell\in\WFF\),
\[
\ell\text{ is a literal}
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists P\in\Prop)(\ell=P\text{ or }\ell=\neg P).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\ell\in\mathsf{Literal}
\]
means that \(\ell\) is an atomic propositional variable or the negation of one
atomic propositional variable.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Literals are the indivisible signed atoms used in normal forms. They remember
which propositional variable is being tested and whether it appears positively
or negatively.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex: The formulas \(P\), \(Q\), \(\neg P\), and \(\neg Q\) are literals.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formulas \(P\land Q\), \(P\lor Q\), and \(\neg(P\land Q)\) are not
literals. The last formula is negated, but it negates a compound formula rather
than a single propositional variable.

nodes.name: Complementary Literals
nodes.statement_display:
Two literals are \emph{complementary} if they are \(P\) and \(\neg P\) for the
same propositional variable \(P\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For literals \(\ell_1,\ell_2\),
\[
\ell_1\text{ and }\ell_2\text{ are complementary}
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists P\in\Prop)
\bigl((\ell_1=P\land \ell_2=\neg P)
\lor
(\ell_1=\neg P\land \ell_2=P)\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{ComplementaryLiterals}(\ell_1,\ell_2)
\]
means that the two literals name the same propositional variable with opposite
signs.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Complementary literals are the local contradiction pattern inside clauses and
terms. The pair \(P,\neg P\) is tied to one variable, not merely to two formulas
with opposite truth values under a particular assignment.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
The literals \(P\) and \(\neg P\) are complementary, as are \(Q\) and
\(\neg Q\).

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex: The literals \(P\) and \(\neg Q\) are not complementary unless \(P=Q\).

\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists P\in\Prop)
\bigl((\ell_1=P\land \ell_2=\neg P)
\lor
(\ell_1=\neg P\land \ell_2=P)\bigr).
\]
logical_blocks.predicate_reading:
\[
\operatorname{ComplementaryLiterals}(\ell_1,\ell_2)
\]
means that the two literals name the same propositional variable with opposite
signs.
logical_blocks.interpretation:
Complementary literals are the local contradiction pattern inside clauses and
terms. The pair \(P,\neg P\) is tied to one variable, not merely to two formulas
with opposite truth values under a particular assignment.
logical_blocks.examples:
The literals \(P\) and \(\neg P\) are complementary, as are \(Q\) and
\(\neg Q\).
logical_blocks.non_examples: The literals \(P\) and \(\neg Q\) are not complementary unless \(P=Q\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
A formula \(C\in\WFF\) is a clause if there are literals
\(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n\) with \(n\ge 1\) such that
\[
C=\ell_1\lor\cdots\lor\ell_n.
\]
The empty clause is treated separately as the empty disjunction.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
C\in\mathsf{Clause}
\]
means that \(C\) is built by finitely disjoining literals.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A clause records a finite list of literal-level alternatives. It is satisfied
when at least one of its literals is true.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formulas \(P\lor Q\), \(P\lor\neg Q\), and
\(\neg P\lor Q\lor R\) are clauses.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formula \(P\land Q\) is not a clause, because its top-level connective is a
conjunction. The formula \(\neg(P\lor Q)\) is not a clause, because its negation
has not been pushed down to the literal level.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
The empty clause is the disjunction over no literals and has truth value

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A nonempty clause is true when at least one listed literal is true. With no
literals listed, there is no witness to make the disjunction true, so the empty
clause is the false boundary case for clauses.

nodes.statement_display:
A formula is in \emph{negation normal form} if it uses only propositional
variables, negated propositional variables, conjunction, and disjunction, and
every negation occurs immediately before a propositional variable.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For a formula \(\varphi\in\WFF\),
\[
\varphi\text{ is in negation normal form}
\Longleftrightarrow
\varphi\text{ is built from literals using only }\land\text{ and }\lor.
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\varphi\in\mathsf{NegationNormalForm}
\]
means that \(\varphi\) has no conditionals, no biconditionals, and no negation
outside the literal level.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Negation normal form is the first cleanup stage for propositional formulas.
It does not force a formula to be a disjunction of terms or a conjunction of
clauses; it only restricts the available connectives and pushes negation down
to propositional variables.

normal form, and the last has a negation applied to a compound formula.

nodes.text_preview: The \emph{NNF conversion procedure} converts a propositional formula to an equivalent formula in negation normal form by the following steps: \begin{enumerate} \item eliminate biconditionals using biconditional equivalence laws; \item elimi

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
Starting with \(\varphi\in\WFF\), repeatedly apply the equivalences
\[
\alpha\leftrightarrow\beta
\equiv
(\alpha\to\beta)\land(\beta\to\alpha),
\qquad
\alpha\to\beta\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\beta,
\]
\[
\neg\neg\alpha\equiv\alpha,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\land\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\lor\neg\beta,
\qquad
\neg(\alpha\lor\beta)\equiv\neg\alpha\land\neg\beta,
\]
until negations occur only immediately before propositional variables and only
\(\land\) and \(\lor\) remain above the literal level.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
(\varphi,\psi)\in\mathsf{NNFConversionProcedure}
\]
means that \(\psi\) is obtained from \(\varphi\) by eliminating
biconditionals and conditionals, removing double negations, and pushing
remaining negations inward.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The procedure is a syntax-directed rewrite process. Each rewrite step is backed
by a logical equivalence law, so the output formula has the same truth
conditions as the input formula.

nodes.name: Semantic Classification by Normal Forms
nodes.statement_display:
Normal forms give finite certificates for semantic classification. For any
formula \(\varphi\in\WFF\):
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\varphi\) is
  \hyperref[def:satisfiable-formula-propositional-logic]{satisfiable} if and
  only if some
  \hyperref[def:disjunctive-normal-form-propositional-logic]{DNF} formula
  equivalent to \(\varphi\) has a satisfiable conjunction term.
  \item \(\varphi\) is a
  \hyperref[def:contradiction-propositional-logic]{contradiction} if and only
  if some DNF formula equivalent to \(\varphi\) has no satisfiable conjunction
  term.
  \item \(\varphi\) is a
  \hyperref[def:tautology-propositional-logic]{tautology} if and only if some
  \hyperref[def:conjunctive-normal-form-propositional-logic]{CNF} formula
  equivalent to \(\varphi\) has no falsifiable clause.
  \item \(\varphi\) is a
  \hyperref[def:contingency-propositional-logic]{contingency} if and only if it
  is satisfiable and not a tautology.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The truth-table method classifies \(\varphi\) by evaluating every row directly.
The normal-form method first rewrites \(\varphi\) into an equivalent DNF or CNF
formula and then checks the finite terms or clauses. Canonical normal forms
connect the two approaches: canonical DNF is built from true rows, and
canonical CNF is built from false rows.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
DNF is naturally witness-producing. A satisfiable term gives an explicit way
to make the whole disjunction true. CNF is naturally suited for clause
checking: each clause is a local obstruction to falsifying the whole
conjunction. This clause-centered view is also the starting point for later
resolution methods.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
v\in\mathsf{TruthAssignment}
\Longleftrightarrow
v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
v\in\mathsf{TruthAssignment}
\]
means that \(v\) assigns exactly one truth value to each propositional variable.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A truth assignment gives semantic values to the atomic formulas. The recursive
truth conditions for the connectives then determine the truth value of every
well-formed formula.

support_blocks.title: Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
If \(\Prop=\{P_1,P_2,P_3,\ldots\}\), then a truth assignment may satisfy
\[
v(P_1)=\True,\qquad v(P_2)=\False,\qquad v(P_3)=\True,
\]
with values assigned to every remaining propositional variable.

support_blocks.title: Non-Examples
support_blocks.body_tex:
A partial assignment that gives values only to \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) is not a truth
assignment on \(\Prop\). It may be useful for local computations, but it is not a
function \(\Prop\to\mathbb{B}\).

nodes.name: Extension of a Truth Assignment to Formulas
nodes.statement_display:
Let
\[
v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B}
\]
be a truth assignment. The \emph{extension} of \(v\) to well-formed formulas is
the function
\[
\widehat v:\WFF\to\mathbb{B}
\]
defined recursively as follows:
\[
\widehat v(P)=v(P)
\quad\text{for every }P\in\Prop,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\neg\varphi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\False,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\land\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ and }
\widehat v(\psi)=\True,
\]
\[
\widehat v(\varphi\lor\psi)=\True
\Longleftrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\True
\text{ or }
\widehat v(\psi)=\True,

support_blocks.body_tex:
For every truth assignment \(v:\Prop\to\mathbb{B}\), its extension is a function

\]

\]
means that \(\widehat v\) is the recursively defined truth-value function on
\(\WFF\) induced by the atomic truth assignment \(v\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The original assignment \(v\) gives truth values only to propositional variables.
The extension \(\widehat v\) evaluates every formula by following the formula's
syntactic construction.

nodes.name: Truth Table
nodes.statement_display:

\[

\]
and a final column recording the value of \(\widehat v(\varphi)\) for any truth assignment \(v\) extending \(a\).

=
w|_{\operatorname{Var}(\varphi)}
\Longrightarrow
\widehat v(\varphi)=\widehat w(\varphi).
\]

nodes.name: Logical Connective
nodes.statement_display:
The standard primitive propositional connectives are
\[
\neg,\qquad \land,\qquad \lor,\qquad \to,\qquad \leftrightarrow.
\]
The connective \(\neg\) is unary. The connectives \(\land,\lor,\to,\leftrightarrow\) are binary.

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{Symbol} & \text{Name} & \text{Arity} & \text{Formation pattern} & \text{Reading}\\
\hline
\neg & \text{negation} & \text{unary} & \neg\varphi & \text{not }\varphi\\
\land & \text{conjunction} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\land\psi) & \varphi\text{ and }\psi\\
\lor & \text{disjunction} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\lor\psi) & \varphi\text{ or }\psi\\
\to & \text{conditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\to\psi) & \text{if }\varphi,\text{ then }\psi\\
\leftrightarrow & \text{biconditional} & \text{binary} & (\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi) & \varphi\text{ iff }\psi
\end{array}
\]
