nodes.text_preview: Let $A$ and $B$ be ordered arithmetic systems. A map $\varphi:A\to B$ is an \emph{embedding} exactly when $\varphi$ is injective and structure-preserving and is an order embedding.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\varphi \text{ is an embedding}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow \Bigl(\varphi \text{ is injective}\land \varphi \text{ is structure-preserving}\\
&\qquad\land \forall a,a'\in A\;(a<_A a'\Leftrightarrow\varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a'))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{NumberSystemEmbedding}(\varphi,A,B,\mathcal{S})
\]
means that $\varphi$ is injective, preserves the selected structure $\mathcal{S}$, and preserves and reflects the selected order.

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\varphi \text{ is not an embedding}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(\exists a,a'\in A\;(a\neq a'\land \varphi(a)=\varphi(a'))\\
&\qquad\lor\ \varphi \text{ fails to preserve a constant, sum, or product}\\
&\qquad\lor\ \exists a,a'\in A\;\bigl((a<_A a'\land \neg(\varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')))
\lor(\varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')\land \neg(a<_A a'))\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.] An embedding can fail by losing distinctness, by failing to preserve selected algebraic structure, or by failing to preserve and reflect order.
  \item[Injectivity fails.]
  \[
  \exists a,a'\in A\;(a\ne a'\land \varphi(a)=\varphi(a')).
  \]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{Injective}(\varphi).
  \]
  \item[Algebraic preservation fails.]
  \[
  \text{$\varphi$ fails to preserve a selected constant or selected operation.}
  \]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{StructurePreservingMap}(\varphi,A,B,\mathcal{S}).
  \]
  \item[Order embedding fails.]
  \[
  \exists a,a'\in A\;\bigl((a<_A a'\land \neg(\varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')))
  \lor(\varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')\land \neg(a<_A a'))\bigr).
  \]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{OrderEmbedding}(\varphi,A,B,<).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
An embedding is the precise meaning of ``$A$ sits inside $B$.'' It is injective, so distinct elements stay distinct; it preserves the arithmetic and reflects the order, so the copy of $A$ inside $B$ behaves exactly as $A$ did. This is what licenses treating $2\in\mathbb{N}$ and $2\in\mathbb{R}$ as ``the same number.''


Most embeddings after $\mathbb{W}$ transport the \emph{ordered ring/field}
structure: constants, the two operations, and order. The first bridge
$\mathbb{N}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{W}$ is slightly different because
$\mathbb{N}$ is one-based and carries Peano successor. That local theorem is
proved in the whole-number chapter. In every case, induction is not transported
to the larger target: the phrase ``the naturals sit inside the integers'' must
not be read as carrying induction across all of $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.statement_display: Let $\varphi:A\to B$ be an embedding. The \emph{image} of $\varphi$ is the set $\varphi(A)=\{\,\varphi(a) : a\in A\,\}\subseteq B$, equipped with the selected constants, operations, and order of $B$ restricted to $\varphi(A)$.

nodes.name: Embeddings Identify a System with Its Image
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\varphi:A\to B$ be an embedding of ordered arithmetic systems relative to
a selected source structure. Then the corestriction $\varphi:A\to\varphi(A)$
is an isomorphism onto its image: it is a bijection that preserves and reflects
the selected constants, operations, and order. Consequently $A$ may be
identified with the corresponding substructure $\varphi(A)\subseteq B$.

nodes.name: Extended Real Addition
nodes.statement_display:
If $x+y$ is defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, then it agrees with ordinary
real addition when $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, and satisfies
\[
x+(+\infty)=+\infty,\qquad x+(-\infty)=-\infty
\]
whenever these expressions are defined.

z=x+y.
\]

nodes.name: Positive cone
nodes.statement_display:
Let $K$ be an arithmetic system with addition, multiplication, and zero. A
subset $P\subset K$ is called a \emph{positive cone} if it satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item if $a,b\in P$, then $a+b\in P$;
  \item if $a,b\in P$, then $ab\in P$;
  \item for every $a\in K$, exactly one of the following holds:
  \[
  a\in P,
  \qquad
  a=0,
  \qquad
  -a\in P.
  \]
\end{enumerate}
The strict order associated to $P$ is
\[
a<b \iff b-a\in P.
\]

nodes.name: Two-sided successor construction data
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{two-sided successor construction data} consists of a carrier \(Z\),
a distinguished element \(0\in Z\), and two total functions
\[
\mathsf{succ},\mathsf{pred}:Z\to Z
\]
such that
\[
\mathsf{pred}(\mathsf{succ}(x))=x
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathsf{succ}(\mathsf{pred}(x))=x
\]
for every \(x\in Z\), together with the decomposition
\[
Z=\{0\}\sqcup P\sqcup N
\]
where \(P\) is generated from \(\mathsf{succ}(0)\) by successor and
\(N\) is generated from \(\mathsf{pred}(0)\) by predecessor.

nodes.name: Two-sided induction and recursion
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(A\) be a predicate on \(Z\). If \(A(0)\), \(A(x)\Rightarrow
A(\mathsf{succ}(x))\), and \(A(x)\Rightarrow A(\mathsf{pred}(x))\)
for every \(x\in Z\), then \(A(x)\) holds for every \(x\in Z\).
Moreover, any value at zero and mutually inverse successor and predecessor
steps determine a unique recursive function out of \(Z\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
A property holds everywhere on \(Z\) once it holds at zero and propagates both
forward and backward; a recursive definition on \(Z\) is determined by its
zero value and compatible forward and backward steps.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is why the ray decomposition matters. To prove something for every
integer, prove it at zero, along the positive ray, and along the negative ray.
To define an operation recursively, the forward and backward clauses must
agree at the places where the rays meet zero.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formal-difference construction begins with pairs and an equivalence
relation. Tao emphasizes expressions \(a{--}b\); Mendelson emphasizes
equivalence classes of pairs and develops more abstract algebra around them.
The two-sided construction begins instead with the geometry of the integer
line. It avoids quotient well-definedness, but it requires explicit recursive
definitions and many transport lemmas for successor and predecessor.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
This section is therefore not a replacement for the standard construction. It
is a worked example of construction verification: choose a target, propose
data, state the axioms, build operations, prove the laws, and finally compare
the result with the already accepted system.

nodes.name: Mendelson 4.3 --- Positivity set construction
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(R\) be an integral domain with \(0\neq 1\). If
\(\mathcal{P}\subseteq R\) excludes \(0\), trichotomizes each element by
membership in \(\mathcal{P}\), equality to \(0\), or membership of its
negative, and is closed under addition and multiplication, then
\[
  x<y \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in\mathcal{P}
\]
defines an ordered integral domain whose positive set is \(\mathcal{P}\).

nodes.name: Tao integer expression
nodes.statement_display:
An integer expression in Tao's construction is a placeholder \(a {-\!\!-} b\)
with \(a,b\in\mathbb{N}\). Two placeholders are equal when
\[
  a {-\!\!-} b = c {-\!\!-} d
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  a+d=c+b.
\]
The collection of equivalence classes is denoted \(\mathbb{Z}\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The definition replaces the circular phrase \(a-b\) with a formal pair and an
equality criterion that only uses arithmetic already available in
\(\mathbb{N}\). The construction pays the equivalence-relation cost once and
then supports uniform definitions of operations on classes.

support_blocks.title: Notation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The symbol \(--\) is scaffolding notation. After subtraction is defined on
\(\mathbb{Z}\), the expression \(a {-\!\!-} b\) agrees with the genuine
difference \(a-b\).

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
This presentation contrasts with the signed-natural description of integers.
The signed-natural picture is intuitive, but it forces repeated case splits
for addition, multiplication, and order. The quotient construction centralizes
those checks in the equivalence relation and well-definedness lemmas.

nodes.name: Tao 4.1.3 --- Addition and multiplication are well-defined
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(a,b,a',b',c,d\in\mathbb{N}\). If
\((a {-\!\!-} b)=(a' {-\!\!-} b')\), then
\begin{align*}
  (a {-\!\!-} b) + (c {-\!\!-} d)
    &= (a' {-\!\!-} b') + (c {-\!\!-} d), \\
  (a {-\!\!-} b)(c {-\!\!-} d)
    &= (a' {-\!\!-} b')(c {-\!\!-} d),
\end{align*}
and similarly when the second representative is replaced by an equal one.

nodes.name: Tao 4.1.5 --- Trichotomy of integers
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(x\in\mathbb{Z}\). Exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(x=0\).
  \item \(x=n\) for some positive natural number \(n\).
  \item \(x=-n\) for some positive natural number \(n\).
\end{enumerate}
In the second case \(x\) is positive, and in the third case \(x\) is negative.

nodes.name: Tao 4.1.11 --- Properties of order on \(\mathbb{Z}\)
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}\). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(a>b\) if and only if \(a-b\) is a positive natural number.
  \item If \(a>b\), then \(a+c>b+c\).
  \item If \(a>b\) and \(c\) is a positive integer, then \(ac>bc\).
  \item If \(a>b\), then \(-a<-b\).
  \item If \(a>b\) and \(b>c\), then \(a>c\).
  \item Exactly one of \(a>b\), \(a<b\), and \(a=b\) holds.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Addition on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For each $m \in P$, define the function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
to be the unique function satisfying
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
For $m,n \in P$, define
\[
m+n \coloneqq f_m(n).
\]

  is simply a value of $P$ different from $f_m(n)$.

  &x \neq m+n
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \underbrace{x \neq f_m(n)}_{\text{candidate value disagrees with the recursive output}}.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
The theorem shows that the recursive clauses for addition determine exactly one
right-input map for each fixed left input. The addition operation is therefore
not assumed; it is constructed from the successor map by recursion.


This is the house-style well-definedness form of addition obtained by applying
the Peano recursion theorem in the manner of Feferman's construction of
arithmetic operations \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{N}$ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
  \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
  $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
  \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
  \item \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
  \item \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: $\mathbb{N}$ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
  \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
  $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
  \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
  $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
  \item \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
  $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.

nodes.name: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

\operatorname{WellDefinedBinaryOperation}(\cdot_P,P).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The recursive clauses for multiplication determine exactly one right-input map
for each fixed left input. The multiplication operation is therefore
constructed from recursion and addition rather than assumed at the outset.


This is the house-style well-definedness form of multiplication obtained by
applying the Peano recursion theorem in the manner of Feferman's construction
of arithmetic operations \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Strict inequality fails exactly when no additive witness in $P$ carries
  $a$ to $b$. In that case, every nontrivial additive step from $a$ misses
  $b$.
  \item[Quantified failure.]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  &\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } a,b \in P.\\
  &a \not< b
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \underbrace{\forall c \in P\;(b \neq a+c)}_{\text{every proposed additive witness fails}}.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

  \item[Exposition.]

  strictly below $b$, and $a$ is not equal to $b$. Thus $b$ neither lies ahead
  of $a$ nor coincides with it.

  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Exponentiation is repeated multiplication in the same sense that multiplication
is repeated addition. The base $a$ is the fixed left factor; the exponent $n$
counts how many times $a$ is multiplied together. The recursive definition
propagates rightward: $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a^1 \cdot a = a \cdot a$, and so on.

Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
h_a:P\to P
\]
such that
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(a,n)\longmapsto a^n\coloneqq h_a(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A positive exponent does not collapse the strict order between bases. Since
the exponent is a natural number, exponentiation repeatedly multiplies by
positive factors and preserves the order information.


This is the house-style common-exponent comparison theorem corresponding to
Feferman's natural-number exponent laws \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Strict growth in the exponent occurs exactly when the base is beyond the
multiplicative identity. If the base is $1$, all powers are $1$; if the base
is larger than $1$, each successor step in the exponent multiplies by a factor
that strictly increases the value.


This is the house-style common-base comparison theorem corresponding to
Feferman's exponent-order theorem \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.text_preview: Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $2 \coloneqq S(1)$. For every $n \in P$, \[ n < 2^n. \]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\forall n \in P\;(n < 2^n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The base case $1 < 2 = 2^1$ holds by definition of $2$ and the strict order.
For the inductive step, assume $n < 2^n$. Then $2^{S(n)} = 2^n \cdot 2$.
Since $2^n > n \ge 1$, it follows that
$2^n \cdot 2 > n \cdot 2 = n + n > n + 1 = S(n)$,
where the last step uses $n \ge 1$ so $n + n > n + 1$. Hence $S(n) < 2^{S(n)}$.
The inequality $n < 2^n$ is the threshold that distinguishes the growth regimes
and reappears in every comparison between polynomial and exponential bounds.

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
The well-ordering principle would fail if some nonempty subset of $P$ had
  no least element. That means for every candidate minimum, a strictly smaller
  element of the subset exists, producing an infinite strictly descending
  chain in $P$. Induction rules this out.

modes.title: No least element.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The well-ordering principle is the order-theoretic complement to induction.
Induction says one can build up: start at $1$ and keep stepping forward.
Well-ordering says one can always descend to a minimum: any nonempty set has
a floor. Proof strategies that use well-ordering typically assume a property
fails somewhere, form the set of failures, extract its minimum by
well-ordering, and derive a contradiction from the minimality of that element.

nodes.name: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
  $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
  for all $n \in P$.
  \item The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
  if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
  $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
  \item The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
  element with respect to $\le$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Induction proves well-ordering by contrapositive: if a nonempty set $A$ had
no least element, the set of non-members of $A$ would be inductive, forcing
$A = \varnothing$, a contradiction. Well-ordering proves induction by forming
the set of elements where $\varphi$ fails and, if nonempty, extracting a
least failure to derive a contradiction with the successor step.

nodes.name: Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
A triple $(P,S,1)$ is called a \emph{Peano system} exactly when $P$ is a set,
$1 \in P$, $S : P \to P$ is a function, and the following axioms hold:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[\textbf{P1.}] $1 \in P$.
  \item[\textbf{P2.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
  \item[\textbf{P3.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
  \item[\textbf{P4.}] For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
  \item[\textbf{P5.}] If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
  \[
    \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
  \]
  then $A=P$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P \land S : P \to P \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading

\[
\operatorname{PeanoSystem}(P,S,1).
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  A triple $(P,S,1)$ fails to be a Peano system if the distinguished element
  does not lie in the underlying set, if the successor map leaves the set, if
  the successor hits $1$, if the successor identifies two distinct elements,
  or if there exists a proper subset of $P$ that contains $1$ and is closed
  under successor.
  \item[Axiom failure.]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{PeanoSystem}(P,S,1).
  \]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \neg\,\text{$(P,S,1)$ is a Peano system}
  \Longrightarrow\;&
  1 \notin P \\
  &\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n) \notin P) \\
  &\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n)=1) \\
  &\lor \exists m,n \in P\;(m \neq n \land S(m)=S(n)) \\
  &\lor \exists A \subseteq P\;
  \bigl(1 \in A \land
  \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A)
  \land A \neq P\bigr).
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A Peano system is the abstract data of counting: an underlying set, a first
element, and a successor operation satisfying the usual non-collision and
induction principles. The purpose of the definition is to isolate the ambient
object before the individual axioms are recorded and used one by one.


The five displayed clauses are the house-style Peano-system presentation of
Peano's axiomatization of arithmetic \citep{PeanoArithmeticesPrincipia1889}.
They are stated here in structural form so that later definitions and proofs
can refer directly to the successor and induction clauses.

support_blocks.title: Source comparison
support_blocks.body_tex:
This definition corresponds closely to Definition 3.1 in
Feferman, where Peano systems are introduced as the abstract structural
framework underlying the positive integers. The present notes expand the
definition into explicit quantified, failure-mode, and decomposition forms in
order to support later logical analysis and dependency extraction.
\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{InductionPrinciple}(P,S,1).
\]

support_blocks.title: Contrapositive quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\neg\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n)
\Longrightarrow
\neg\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem converts the subset form of induction into the predicate form
used in ordinary arithmetic arguments. A property propagates through the
entire Peano system once it holds at the distinguished first element and is
preserved by successor. The theorem therefore turns the structural induction
axiom into a proof principle for arbitrary predicates on $P$.

support_blocks.title: Source comparison
support_blocks.body_tex:
Peano's axiomatization includes induction as part of the natural-number
structure. Feferman derives the working form of mathematical induction from
the subset formulation of the Peano axioms immediately after Theorem 3.3 in
Chapter 3. The present notes formalize that induction principle as an explicit
reusable theorem. \citep{PeanoArithmeticesPrincipia1889}; \citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A predecessor of $x$ is an element whose successor is $x$. This language
isolates the inverse-looking question attached to the successor map without
assuming that successor is globally invertible.

support_blocks.body_tex:
Every element of a Peano system is reached by starting at the distinguished
first element and moving forward by successor. The only possible exception to
having a predecessor is the element $1$ itself.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  The biconditional can fail in two ways: a non-initial element can fail to
  have a unique predecessor, or the distinguished first element can have a
  unique predecessor.
  \item[Characterization failure.]
  \[
  \neg\forall x \in P\;\bigl(x\neq 1 \Longleftrightarrow
  \exists! u \in P\;(S(u)=x)\bigr).
  \]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  &\exists x \in P\;\Bigl(
  \underbrace{\bigl(x\neq 1 \land
  (\forall u \in P\;(S(u)\neq x)
  \lor
  \exists u,v \in P\;(S(u)=x \land S(v)=x \land u\neq v))\bigr)}_
  {\text{non-initial element lacks a unique predecessor}}\\
  &\qquad\qquad\lor
  \underbrace{\bigl(x=1 \land \exists u \in P\;(S(u)=x \land
  \forall v \in P\;(S(v)=x \Longrightarrow v=u))\bigr)}_
  {\text{the first element has a unique predecessor}}
  \Bigr).
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

examples.label: Why the base case is forced
examples.title: Why the base case is forced
examples.body_tex:
For the first element, the theorem says
\[
S(1)\neq 1.
\]
This is exactly the axiom that the distinguished element is not a successor:
there is no element $x\in P$ with $S(x)=1$. In particular, taking $x=1$
would be impossible, so $S(1)\neq 1$.

examples.label: Why the induction step uses injectivity
examples.title: Why the induction step uses injectivity
examples.body_tex:
Suppose the induction hypothesis gives $S(n)\neq n$. To prove the next case,
we must show
\[
S(S(n))\neq S(n).
\]
If equality held, injectivity of $S$ would let us cancel the outer successor
and conclude $S(n)=n$, contradicting the induction hypothesis. Thus the
property propagates from $n$ to $S(n)$.

nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{Presburger signature} is the first-order signature
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pres}} = \{0, S, +, <, =\},
\]
where $0$ is a constant symbol, $S$ is a unary function symbol, $+$ is a
binary function symbol, and $<$ and $=$ are binary relation symbols.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The Presburger signature names addition and order, but it deliberately omits
multiplication as a function symbol. This makes Presburger arithmetic a theory
of the additive structure of the natural numbers rather than a theory of full
arithmetic.

of the additive structure of the natural numbers rather than a theory of full
arithmetic.

nodes.name: Presburger Arithmetic
nodes.statement_display:
\emph{Presburger arithmetic} is the first-order theory of the natural numbers
in the Presburger signature. Its intended structure is
\[
(\mathbb{N},0,S,+,<,=),
\]
and its axioms describe the behavior of zero, successor, addition, order, and
induction for formulas written in the language
$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pres}}$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Presburger arithmetic isolates the part of arithmetic governed by addition.
It is strong enough to express linear equations, congruences, and order
properties of natural numbers, but it cannot directly express multiplication
as a primitive operation. The later Peano-system material supplies the more
general recursive framework from which addition, multiplication, order, and
induction are developed structurally.

  &\lor \underbrace{g \text{ is not a function } W\to W}_{\text{invalid update rule}}.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Iterator Relation
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. A
relation $R\subseteq P\times W$ is called an \emph{iterator relation} for
$(W,c,g)$ exactly when
\[
(1,c)\in R
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;\forall w\in W\;
\bigl((n,w)\in R\Longrightarrow (S(n),g(w))\in R\bigr).
\]

Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  An iterator relation fails if it is not a relation inside $P\times W$, if
  it omits the required base pair, or if it is not closed under the iterator
  step.
  \item[Invalid relation.]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{IteratorRelation}(R,(P,S,1),W,c,g).
  \]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  R \text{ is not an iterator relation for } (W,c,g)
  \Longleftrightarrow\;&
  \underbrace{R\not\subseteq P\times W}_{\text{wrong ambient relation}}\\
  &\lor \underbrace{(1,c)\notin R}_{\text{base pair missing}}\\
  &\lor \underbrace{\exists n\in P\;\exists w\in W\;
  \bigl((n,w)\in R\land (S(n),g(w))\notin R\bigr)}_{\text{step closure fails}}.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Minimal Iterator Relation
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The \emph{minimal iterator relation} for $(W,c,g)$ is
\[
R^*
=
\bigcap\{R\subseteq P\times W : R \text{ is an iterator relation for }
(W,c,g)\}.
\]

  \]
\end{description}

by the base pair and the successor closure rule. This is the $R^*$ construction
used in Feferman's proof of recursive definition, and in the related
set-theoretic presentations cited here
\citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964,hrbacek_jech1999,chi_recursion_wustl}.

$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. If $(n,w_0)\in R^*$ and
$(n,w_1)\in R^*$, then $w_0=w_1$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\forall n\in P\;\forall w_0,w_1\in W\;
\bigl((n,w_0)\in R^*\land (n,w_1)\in R^*\Longrightarrow w_0=w_1\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{FunctionalRelation}(R^*,P,W).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\exists n\in P\;\exists w_0,w_1\in W\;
\bigl((n,w_0)\in R^*\land (n,w_1)\in R^*\land w_0\neq w_1\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Forced value uniqueness fails exactly when one stage is assigned two
  distinct values by the minimal iterator relation.
  \item[Two forced values.]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{FunctionalRelation}(R^*,P,W).
  \]
  \[
  \exists n\in P\;\exists w_0,w_1\in W\;
  \bigl((n,w_0)\in R^*\land (n,w_1)\in R^*\land w_0\neq w_1\bigr).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Contrapositive quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\exists n\in P\;\exists w_0,w_1\in W\;
\bigl((n,w_0)\in R^*\land (n,w_1)\in R^*\land w_0\neq w_1\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
R^* \text{ is not functional at every stage}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
No stage can be forced to carry two different values. This is the key
determinacy step in the minimal-relation construction used to turn recursive
specifications into functions \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.name: Determinism of the Minimal Iterator Relation
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it, and let
$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. For each $n\in P$, there is at most one
$w\in W$ such that $(n,w)\in R^*$.

support_blocks.body_tex:

recursive definition: after determinacy gives at most one value at each stage,
completeness gives at least one value at each stage
\citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
$f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\forall f,h:P\to W\;\Bigl(&
f(1)=c\land h(1)=c\\
&\land \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))\\
&\land \forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n)))
\Longrightarrow f=h\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\forall f,h:P\to W\;
\bigl(\operatorname{IteratorFunction}(f,(P,S,1),W,c,g)
\land \operatorname{IteratorFunction}(h,(P,S,1),W,c,g)
\Longrightarrow f=h\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\exists f,h:P\to W\;\Bigl(&
f(1)=c\land h(1)=c\\
&\land \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))\\
&\land \forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n)))
\land f\neq h\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Uniqueness fails exactly when two distinct functions satisfy the same base
  clause and the same successor clause.
  \item[Two iterator functions.]
  \[
  \neg\forall f,h:P\to W\;
  \bigl(\operatorname{IteratorFunction}(f,(P,S,1),W,c,g)
  \land \operatorname{IteratorFunction}(h,(P,S,1),W,c,g)
  \Longrightarrow f=h\bigr).
  \]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \exists f,h:P\to W\;\Bigl(&
  f(1)=c\land h(1)=c\\
  &\land \forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))\\
  &\land \forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n)))
  \land f\neq h\Bigr).
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Contrapositive quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f\neq h
\Longrightarrow\;&
f(1)\neq c\lor h(1)\neq c\\
&\lor \exists n\in P\;(f(S(n))\neq g(f(n)))\\
&\lor \exists n\in P\;(h(S(n))\neq g(h(n))).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The iterator clauses determine at most one function. Any difference between
two candidate functions must show up as a failure of the base clause or a
failure of one of the successor clauses.

nodes.name: Peano Iterator Theorem
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
Then there exists a unique function $f:P\to W$ such that
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The theorem says that iterator data is sufficient to turn a recursive
specification into a genuine definition: there is exactly one graph and hence
exactly one function satisfying the base and successor clauses.

support_blocks.title: Historical note
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is the one-based Peano-system version of the iterator theorem in
\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964,MendelsonNumberSystemsFoundationsAnalysis,simpson2011peanosystems}.
It is also the set-theoretic instance of the natural numbers object universal
property \citep{lawvere1969adjointness}; Dedekind's recursion theorem is the
classical ancestor \citep{dedekind1901essays}.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.

nodes.name: General Recursive Function
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi:P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. A function $f:P\to W$
is called the \emph{general recursive function determined by $(W,c,\Phi)$}
exactly when
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n))).
\]

nodes.name: Uniqueness of General Recursive Functions
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi:P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. If $f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=\Phi(n,h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Peano Systems up to Isomorphism
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that
\[
\theta(1_P)=1_Q
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(\theta(S_P(n))=S_Q(\theta(n))).
\]
Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.

elements may be named differently, but the distinguished first element and
successor structure determine the translation.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}\text{ be nonempty and bounded.}\\
&\inf A+\inf B\le \inf(A+B)
\quad\land\quad
\sup(A+B)\le \sup A+\sup B.
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(t_A,A)\land \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(t_B,B)
\land
\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_A,A)\land \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_B,B)
\Longrightarrow
t_A+t_B\le \inf(A+B)\le \sup(A+B)\le s_A+s_B.
\]

\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.

\lor
\bigl[\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_A,A)\land \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_B,B)\land s_A+s_B<\sup(A+B)\bigr]
\]
is a contradictory configuration.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&u\text{ is an upper bound of }A\text{ in }S
\Longleftrightarrow
u\in S\text{ and }\forall x\in A\;(x\le_S u),\\
&u\text{ is an upper bound of }A\text{ in }T
\Longleftrightarrow
u\in T\text{ and }\forall x\in A\;(x\le_T u).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{UpperBound}_S(u,A)
\Longleftrightarrow
u\in S\land \forall x\in A\;(x\le_S u).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\text{The phrase ``}u\text{ is an upper bound of }A\text{''}
\]
is not well-determined until the ambient ordered set and its order relation are fixed.

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{WellDefined}(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A))
\]
when the ambient order is omitted.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex: Ambiguity occurs when the same set $A$ is considered inside different ordered ambient sets or under different order relations. The candidate bound may belong to one ambient set and not another, or the relevant comparison relation may change.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation

nodes.name: Displacement, Dilation, and Reflection
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $c,\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.  Define
\[
  A+c:=\{a+c:a\in A\},\qquad
  A-c:=\{a-c:a\in A\},\qquad
  \lambda A:=\{\lambda a:a\in A\}.
\]
The set $-A:=(-1)A$ is the \emph{reflection} of $A$ through the origin.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ and } s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&s \text{ satisfies the epsilon characterization of } \sup A\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\forall x\in A\;(x\le s)\Bigr]
\land
\Bigl[\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists a\in A\;(s-\varepsilon<a)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{EpsilonCharacterizationOfSupremum}(s,A,\mathbb{R})
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,\mathbb{R})
\Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{UpperBound}(s,A)
\land
\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists a\in A\;(s-\varepsilon<a).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ and } s\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&s \text{ does not satisfy the epsilon characterization of } \sup A\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\exists x\in A\;(s<x)\Bigr]
\lor
\Bigl[\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall a\in A\;(a\le s-\varepsilon_0)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{EpsilonCharacterizationOfSupremum}(s,A,\mathbb{R})\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\exists x\in A\;(s<x)\Bigr]
\lor
\Bigl[\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall a\in A\;(a\le s-\varepsilon_0)\Bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex: The characterization fails either because $s$ is not an upper bound of $A$, or because $A$ remains at least some positive distance below $s$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{EpsilonCharacterizationOfSupremum}(s,A,\mathbb{R})
=
\underbrace{\exists x\in A\;(s<x)}_{\text{upper-bound failure}}
\;\lor\;
\underbrace{\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall a\in A\;(a\le s-\varepsilon_0)}_{\text{positive gap below }s}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: This condition says that $s$ caps the set from above while points of $A$ approach $s$ from below at every positive scale. The upper-bound clause prevents $A$ from crossing above $s$, and the epsilon clause prevents $s$ from floating strictly above the set. Geometrically, $s$ is a ceiling that the set presses against arbitrarily closely.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This condition says that $t$ sits below the set while points of $A$ approach $t$ from above at every positive scale. The lower-bound clause prevents $A$ from crossing below $t$, and the epsilon clause prevents $t$ from sitting strictly below the set with a positive gap. Geometrically, $t$ is a floor that the set presses against arbitrarily closely from above.


The epsilon characterizations are one way to prove the sharpness part of a
supremum or infimum claim.  After proving the candidate is an upper or lower
bound, one can either compare it with arbitrary bounds directly or build
near-extremal points using an arbitrary $\varepsilon>0$.  The proof-techniques
chapter gives a fuller guide to choosing between these approaches:
\hyperref[subsec:eps-char]{The $\varepsilon$-Characterisation of Suprema and
Infima}.

element $m\in S$ is the \emph{maximum} of $A$ if $m\in A$ and every
element of $A$ is less than or equal to $m$.

nodes.name: Minimum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty.  An
element $m\in S$ is the \emph{minimum} of $A$ if $m\in A$ and every
element of $A$ is greater than or equal to $m$.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty.  If
$m,n\in S$ are both maxima of $A$, then $m=n$.

support_blocks.body_tex:

Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty.  If
$s=\sup A$ and $s\in A$, then $s=\max A$.

nodes.name: Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and let
$s\in S$.  The element $s$ is the \emph{supremum} of $A$ if $s$ is an
upper bound of $A$ and no smaller element of $S$ is an upper bound of
$A$.

Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and let
$s\in S$.  The element $s$ is the \emph{supremum} of $A$ if $s$ is an
upper bound of $A$ and no smaller element of $S$ is an upper bound of
$A$.

nodes.text_preview: Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and let $s\in S$. The element $s$ is the \emph{supremum} of $A$ if $s$ is an upper bound of $A$ and no smaller element of $S$ is an upper bound of $A$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  A\neq\varnothing
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  (\forall x\in A)(x\leq s)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  (\forall u\in S)\bigl[(\forall x\in A)(x\leq u)\Rightarrow s\leq u\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(S,\leq),\qquad
  \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  :=
  \operatorname{UpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \land
  (\forall u\in S)
  \bigl(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\Rightarrow s\leq u\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  A=\varnothing
  \quad\text{or}\quad
  (\exists x\in A)(s<x)
  \quad\text{or}\quad
  (\exists u\in S)\bigl[(\forall x\in A)(x\leq u)\ \text{and}\ u<s\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  \neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \Longleftrightarrow
  A=\varnothing
  \lor
  \neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \lor
  (\exists u\in S)
  \bigl(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  The set may be empty; $s$ may fail to be an upper bound; or $s$ may be an
  upper bound that is not least among upper bounds.

  \item[Mechanism.]
  The first clause is a domain failure.  The second is a bound failure.  The
  third is a sharpness failure witnessed by a strictly smaller upper bound.
  \[
    A=\varnothing
    \quad\text{or}\quad
    (\exists x\in A)(s<x)
    \quad\text{or}\quad
    (\exists u\in S)\bigl[(\forall x\in A)(x\leq u)\ \text{and}\ u<s\bigr].
  \]
  \[
    \neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \Longleftrightarrow
    A=\varnothing
    \lor
    \neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \lor
    (\exists u\in S)
    \bigl(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s\bigr).
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set and let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty.  If
$s,t\in S$ are both suprema of $A$, then $s=t$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would require two distinct least upper bounds for the same
  nonempty set.

  \item[Mechanism.]
  Each candidate is an upper bound and each lies below every upper bound;
  applying these minimality clauses to the other candidate gives both
  $s\leq t$ and $t\leq s$.
  \[
    A\neq\varnothing
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(t,A,P)
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    s\neq t.
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(S,\leq),\qquad
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)\land
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(t,A,P)\land s\neq t.
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Upper Bound Property of the Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and
suppose that $s=\sup A$ exists in $S$.  Then every element of $A$ lies
below $s$:
\[
  (\forall x\in A)(x\leq s).
\]

nodes.name: Subset Inclusion Preserves Upper Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq S$ be nonempty subsets of an ordered set
$(S,\leq)$.  If $u$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound
of $A$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would require a counterexample in the smaller set even though
  the larger set is already bounded by $u$.

  \item[Mechanism.]
  Any counterexample $x\in A$ is also an element of $B$, contradicting the
  upper-bound hypothesis for $B$.
  \[
    A\subseteq B,\quad \operatorname{UpperBound}(u,B,P),
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    (\exists x\in A)(u<x).
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(S,\leq),\qquad
    \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\land
    \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(j,A,P)\land i\neq j.
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.statement_display:

$A\subseteq B$, then $\sup A\leq\sup B$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would mean enlarging a nonempty set lowers its least upper bound.

  \item[Mechanism.]
  The value $\sup B$ bounds $B$, hence bounds $A$; since $\sup A$ is least
  among upper bounds of $A$, $\sup A\leq\sup B$.
  \[
    A\subseteq B,\quad \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_A,A,P),\quad
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_B,B,P),\quad s_B<s_A.
  \]

    \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\land
    \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(j,A,P)\land i\neq j.
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Upper Bound Comparison with the Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
$s=\sup A$.  For $u\in\mathbb{R}$, the number $u$ is an upper bound of
$A$ if and only if $s\leq u$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  A\neq\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  (\forall u\in\mathbb{R})
  \bigl[\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\Longleftrightarrow s\leq u\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(S,\leq),\qquad
  \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)\Longrightarrow
  \forall u\,(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\leftrightarrow s\leq u).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  (\exists u)\bigl[(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s)
  \lor(s\leq u\land\neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P))\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would mean an upper bound below the supremum, or a number above
  the supremum that fails to bound the set.

  \item[Mechanism.]
  Leastness gives the forward implication.  The fact that $s$ bounds $A$
  gives the reverse implication by transitivity.
  \[
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    (\exists u)\bigl[(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s)
    \lor(s\leq u\land\neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P))\bigr].
  \]
  \[

nodes.name: Bound
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$ be nonempty, and let
$b\in S$.  A \emph{bound} of $A$ means a one-sided comparison between $b$
and every element of $A$: either $x\leq b$ for all $x\in A$, or $b\leq x$
for all $x\in A$.

nodes.name: Lower Bound in the Real Line
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and let $\ell\in\mathbb{R}$.  The
element $\ell$ is a \emph{lower bound} of $A$ in the real line if every
element of $A$ is greater than or equal to $\ell$.

displays:
\neg\operatorname{HasArchimedeanProperty}(\mathbb{R})

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The Archimedean Property says that the natural numbers do not stop below any real ceiling. No real number is so large that every natural number remains below it. In this chapter, the result is a consequence of completeness: a bounded copy of $\mathbb{N}$ would have a supremum, and that supremum is contradicted by shifting one natural number upward.

nodes.name: Least Upper Bound Property

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }(S,\le)\text{ be an ordered set}.\\
&S\text{ has the Least Upper Bound Property}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall A\subseteq S\;
\Bigl[
\bigl(A\neq\varnothing \land \exists u\in S\;\forall x\in A\;(x\le u)\bigr)
\rightarrow
\exists s\in S\;\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A)
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

\rightarrow
\exists s\in S\;\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A)
\Bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The Least Upper Bound Property says that upper-bounded nonempty subsets do not point toward missing ceiling elements. Whenever the order supplies at least one upper bound, it also supplies a smallest upper bound in the same ambient set. Failure therefore indicates a hole in the ordered structure rather than a defect in the subset alone.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The completeness axiom asserts that the real line has no order gaps of the least-upper-bound kind. Nonempty sets of real numbers that are bounded above always determine a real number sitting exactly at the least possible ceiling. This is the structural property that distinguishes $\mathbb{R}$ from ordered fields such as $\mathbb{Q}$.

  \land

  \rightarrow

\bigr).
\]

monotone sequence: the supremum or infimum of its range becomes the sequence
limit.

\[
\bigl[\forall (x_n)\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;
(\operatorname{Monotone}((x_n),\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq))\land\operatorname{Bounded}(x_n)
\Rightarrow \operatorname{ConvergesTo}(x_n))\bigr]
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{HasLeastUpperBoundProperty}(\mathbb{R}).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Starting from a nonempty set $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ bounded above, choose an
element of $A$ and an upper bound. Bisect the bracket. Keep the upper endpoint
when the midpoint is still an upper bound; otherwise keep the midpoint as a
new lower endpoint. The two endpoint sequences are bounded and monotone, so
monotone convergence produces a common limiting boundary, which is the
supremum of $A$.

nodes.statement_display:
Over the Archimedean ordered field axioms, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item $\mathbb{R}$ has the least upper bound property.
  \item Every bounded monotone real sequence converges.

  \item Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.
  \item Every Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ converges.
\end{enumerate}

\]

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex: Density fails when some point of $S$ has a positive-radius neighborhood that contains no point of $D$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{IsDense}(D,S)
=
\underbrace{\exists x\in S}_{\text{point not approximated}}
\;\underbrace{\exists \varepsilon_0>0}_{\text{positive exclusion radius}}
\;\underbrace{\forall d\in D\;\bigl(|x-d|\ge \varepsilon_0\bigr)}_{\text{no point of }D\text{ enters the neighborhood}}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Density is an approximation property inside $S$. It does not say that every point of $S$ already belongs to $D$; it says that points of $D$ occur arbitrarily close to every point of $S$. Thus $D$ can be a proper subset of $S$ while still leaving no positive-width gap inside $S$.

nodes.name: Order Dense Subset
nodes.statement_display: Let $X$ be a linearly ordered set and let $A\subseteq X$. The subset $A$ is \emph{order dense in} $X$ if and only if for every $a,b\in X$ with $a<b$ there exists $c\in A$ such that $a<c<b$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }X\text{ be a linearly ordered set and }A\subseteq X.\\
&A\text{ is order dense in }X
\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\rightarrow \exists c\in A\;(a<c<b)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{IsOrderDenseSubset}(A,X)\coloneqq
\forall a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\rightarrow \exists c\in A\;(a<c<b)\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let }X\text{ be a linearly ordered set and }A\subseteq X.\\
&A\text{ is not order dense in }X
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{IsOrderDenseSubset}(A,X)\Longleftrightarrow
\exists a,b\in X\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)\bigr).
\]

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex: Order density fails when there is a nonempty open interval of $X$ that contains no point of $A$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{IsOrderDenseSubset}(A,X)
=
\underbrace{\exists a,b\in X\;(a<b)}_{\text{nonempty interval}}
\;\land\;
\underbrace{\forall c\in A\;(c\le a\lor b\le c)}_{\text{no point of }A\text{ lies between }a\text{ and }b}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Order density is an interval-penetration property. It ignores metric distance and asks only whether every ordered gap contains a point of the subset. A subset can therefore be order dense in $X$ precisely when no nonempty open interval of $X$ is missed entirely by that subset.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{IsOrderDenseSubset}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R})\Longleftrightarrow
\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(a<b\rightarrow \exists q\in\mathbb{Q}\;(a<q<b)\bigr).

\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{IsOrderDenseSubset}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R})\Longleftrightarrow
\exists a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;\bigl(a<b\land \forall q\in\mathbb{Q}\;(q\le a\lor b\le q)\bigr).

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex: The theorem would fail precisely if some nonempty real interval contained no rational number.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
\[
\neg\operatorname{IsOrderDenseSubset}(\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R})
=
\underbrace{\exists a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;(a<b)}_{\text{nonempty real interval}}
\;\land\;
\underbrace{\forall q\in\mathbb{Q}\;(q\le a\lor b\le q)}_{\text{no rational lies inside}}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Rational numbers penetrate every real interval. The theorem does not say that every real number is rational; it says that rational numbers are never separated from a real interval by a positive order gap. This is the interval form of rational density in the real line.

nodes.name: Nested Intervals with Vanishing Length Have Unique Point
nodes.statement_display:

\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[

\land

\Longrightarrow
\exists x\in\mathbb{R}\;

\[
\Delta(fg)(n)=f(n)\Delta g(n)+g(n+1)\Delta f(n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
In continuous calculus, \((fg)' = f'g + fg'\) is symmetric in \(f\)
and \(g\). In discrete calculus the rule is slightly asymmetric: one
factor is evaluated at \(n\) and the other at \(n+1\). This asymmetry
is unavoidable and is a characteristic feature of the discrete setting.
The product rule leads directly to the summation by parts formula:
summing both sides of \(\Delta(fg) = f\,\Delta g + g(E)\,\Delta f\)
over \(k = a\) to \(b-1\) and applying the Fundamental Theorem gives
the formula in the next section.

nodes.name: Summation by Parts
nodes.statement_display:
For functions \(f, g : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}\) and integers \(a \le b\),
\[
\sum_{k=a}^{b-1} f(k)\,\Delta g(k)
=
\Bigl[f(k)g(k)\Bigr]_{k=a}^{k=b}
-
\sum_{k=a}^{b-1} g(k+1)\,\Delta f(k).
\]
That is,
\[
\sum_{k=a}^{b-1} f(k)\,\Delta g(k)
=
f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)
-
\sum_{k=a}^{b-1} g(k+1)\,\Delta f(k).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The continuous integration by parts formula,
\[
\int_a^b f\,dg = \bigl[fg\bigr]_a^b - \int_a^b g\,df,
\]
is recovered from summation by parts by replacing \(\sum\) with
\(\int\) and \(\Delta\) with \(d\). The asymmetry in the discrete
formula --- \(g(k+1)\) rather than \(g(k)\) in the remaining sum ---
reflects the shift inherent in the product rule.
Summation by parts is useful for evaluating sums involving products,
particularly when one factor is easy to sum (as a falling factorial)
and the other is easy to difference. Classic applications include
evaluating \(\sum k r^k\) (where \(f(k) = k\) and
\(\Delta g(k) = r^k\), leading to a geometric-type sum) and establishing
Abel's summation formula.

nodes.name: Forward Difference Operator
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}\).
The \emph{forward difference operator} \(\Delta\) is defined by
\[
\Delta f(n) = f(n+1) - f(n).
\]
The function \(\Delta f\) measures the change in \(f\) when the input
increases by one unit.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem is the discrete analogue of the Fundamental Theorem of
Calculus,
\[
\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b)-f(a).
\]
In continuous calculus, differentiation and integration are inverse
operations. In discrete calculus, the analogous inverse pair is the
difference operator \(\Delta\) and summation. Any sum can be evaluated
by finding a discrete antiderivative of the summand --- just as any
definite integral can be evaluated by finding an antiderivative.
The theorem reduces the problem of computing \(\sum_{k=a}^{b-1} f(k)\)
to the algebraic problem of finding \(F\) with \(\Delta F = f\). Combined
with the falling factorial rules developed in the next section, this
gives a systematic method for evaluating a wide family of sums in
closed form.

The theorem 
expands a power of a sum by counting how many terms choose each
possible number of \(y\)-factors.

set of \(n\), and the theorem describes how a power of a sum expands into
a sum of products.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
In discrete calculus the independent variable moves in \emph{integer steps}
rather than continuously. Change is therefore measured between
successive integer inputs rather than through infinitesimal limits.
The fundamental operator of discrete calculus is the \emph{difference operator}
\[
\Delta f(n)=f(n+1)-f(n),
\]
which plays a role analogous to the derivative in continuous calculus.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
A discrete function is simply another way of viewing a \emph{sequence}.
A sequence \(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots\) is identified with
\[
f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad f(n) = a_n.
\]
Several equivalent notations appear in the literature:
\(f(n)\), \(a_n\), \((a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\), \(\{a_n\}_{n=0}^{\infty}\).
All describe the same object. The functional notation \(f(n)\) is preferred
in discrete calculus because the difference operator acts on it much as a
derivative acts on functions in continuous calculus.

nodes.name: Summation
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(f\) be a function defined on the integers.
For integers \(a \le b\), the expression
\[
\sum_{k=a}^{b} f(k)
\]
denotes the sum \(f(a) + f(a+1) + f(a+2) + \cdots + f(b)\).
The symbol \(\sum\) (Greek capital sigma) represents summation;
\(k\) is the \emph{index of summation}; \(a\) and \(b\) are the
\emph{lower} and \emph{upper limits}; \(f(k)\) is the \emph{summand}.

support_blocks.body_tex:
Every forward-difference row for \(2^n\) reproduces the same function.


Since every finite difference of \(2^n\) is \(2^n\) again, the difference
table of \(2^n\) consists entirely of the sequence \(2^n\) at every level.

reach \(0\) at the \((d+1)\)-th difference row. The non-termination of
the difference table is the signature of a genuinely transcendental discrete
function.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $f:A\to B$, $S,T\subseteq B$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]

\end{enumerate}

operations including complement. Contrast with image: $f(A\cap B)

is not injective. Preimage identities are load-bearing in topology
(preimages of open sets are open) and measure theory (preimages of
measurable sets are measurable).

nodes.name: Centered Open Interval
nodes.statement_display:
Let $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. The
\textbf{centered open interval of radius $\varepsilon$ about $x$} is
\[
  I_\varepsilon(x):=(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)
  =\{y\in\mathbb{R}: |y-x|<\varepsilon\}.
\]
Older sources often call this the $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of $x$ and write
$V_\varepsilon(x)$.

nodes.name: Division of Inequalities Is Not Valid in General
nodes.statement_display:
There exist nonzero real numbers $a,b,c,d$ such that $a>b$ and $c>d$, but
neither

\quad\text{nor}\quad
\frac{c}{a}>\frac{d}{b}
\]
holds.

support_blocks.body_tex:

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The squeeze principle forces equality when a value is simultaneously
bounded above and below by equal quantities.  The continuous analogue
(if $f(x) \le g(x) \le h(x)$ and $f(x) \to L$ and $h(x) \to L$ then
$g(x) \to L$) is the central tool for computing limits.  The algebraic
version stated here is its foundation.

(\sqrt a)^2=a.
\]

nodes.name: Absolute Value
nodes.statement_display:
Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$.  The \emph{absolute value} (or \emph{modulus}) of
$a$ is
\[
  \lvert a \rvert
  \;:=\;
  \begin{cases}
    a  & \text{if } a \ge 0, \\
    -a & \text{if } a < 0.
  \end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, $\lvert a \rvert := \max(a, -a)$.

support_blocks.body_tex:

line it equals the distance from $a$ to $0$: $\lvert a \rvert = d(a, 0)$
under the standard metric.  The two-branch definition partitions
$\mathbb{R}$ at $0$ and reflects negative values to positive ones.

\[

\Bigl(
  \bigl(\exists L\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists N\in\mathbb{N}
  \;\forall n\ge N\;( |x_n-L|<\varepsilon )\bigr)\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow
  \forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists N\in\mathbb{N}\;\forall m,n\ge N
  \;( |x_m-x_n|<\varepsilon )
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

\[

\Bigl(
  \exists L\in\mathbb{R}\;\operatorname{ConvergesTo}(x_n,L)
  \Longrightarrow
  \operatorname{IsCauchy}(x_n)
\Bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation

sufficiently late terms are close to each other. This theorem is the easy
half of the Cauchy criterion.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, let $L\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$. If $x_n\to L$, then $\alpha x_n\to \alpha L$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Multiplying every term by a fixed scalar multiplies the limiting value by the
same scalar. The case $\alpha=0$ collapses the sequence to the constant zero
sequence.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (x_n),(y_n) \text{ be real sequences and let } L,M\in\mathbb{R}.\\
&\bigl[
x_n\to L \;\land\; y_n\to M
\bigr]
\Longrightarrow
\bigl[
x_n+y_n\to L+M
\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\bigl(
\operatorname{ConvergesTo}(x_n,L)
\land
\operatorname{ConvergesTo}(y_n,M)
\bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{ConvergesTo}(x_n+y_n,L+M).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The sum law says that convergent sequences may be added before or after
taking limits. The proof splits a target tolerance into two smaller tolerances,
one for each summand.

nodes.name: Nonzero Limit is Eventually Nonzero

for every $n\ge N$.

nodes.name: Convergence of a Sequence
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. The sequence $(x_n)$ \textbf{converges}
to $L \in \mathbb{R}$ if
\[
    \forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists N \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge N
    \;\bigl(|x_n - L| < \varepsilon\bigr).
\]
The value $L$ is called the \textbf{limit} of $(x_n)$, written
$x_n \to L$ or $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = L$.
A sequence that converges to some $L \in \mathbb{R}$ is called
\textbf{convergent}; otherwise it is called \textbf{divergent}.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
Failure of convergence to a fixed $L$ means that some positive tolerance
cannot be controlled on any tail. The escaped terms may oscillate, drift
monotonically away, or grow without bound, but all such behavior is
captured by the same persistent-tolerance obstruction.
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The quantifier order $\forall \varepsilon \;\exists N \;\forall n \ge N$
encodes a strict dependency: $N$ is permitted to depend on $\varepsilon$,
but not on $n$. This asymmetry is load-bearing. Reversing the outer
quantifiers to $\exists N \;\forall \varepsilon$ would assert that a
single index $N$ controls all tolerances simultaneously, which is a
strictly stronger and generally false condition. The condition
$|x_n - L| < \varepsilon$ is the membership assertion $x_n \in (L -
\varepsilon,\, L + \varepsilon)$; convergence is therefore the statement
that the tail of the sequence is eventually contained in every
centered $\varepsilon$-interval about $L$.

nodes.name: Convergence --- Centered Interval Formulation
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The sequence
$(x_n)$ \textbf{converges} to $L$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the
centered open interval
\[
    I_\varepsilon(L) \;:=\; (L - \varepsilon,\, L + \varepsilon)
\]
contains all but finitely many terms of $(x_n)$; that is,
\[
    \forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists N \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge N
    \;\bigl(x_n \in I_\varepsilon(L)\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The centered interval formulation reframes convergence as a set-containment
condition rather than an inequality condition. The assertion $x_n \in
I_\varepsilon(L)$ is identical to $|x_n - L| < \varepsilon$; the two
definitions are logically equivalent and the choice between them is one
of language, not content. The local-set language is the natural
bridge to the topological formulation: in a general topological space,
open sets replace centered $\varepsilon$-intervals and the definition reads
identically with $I_\varepsilon(L)$ replaced by any open set $U$
containing $L$. The phrase \emph{all but finitely many terms} is the
canonical prose compression of the quantifier block $\exists N \in
\mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge N$, and is standard in the literature.

nodes.name: Equivalence of Convergence Formulations
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The following
statements are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
    \item $x_n \to L$.
    \item $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
          \;\bigl(|x_n - L| < \varepsilon\bigr)$.
    \item $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
          \;\bigl(L - \varepsilon < x_n < L + \varepsilon\bigr)$.
    \item $\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists K \in \mathbb{N} \;\forall n \ge K
          \;\bigl(x_n \in I_\varepsilon(L)\bigr)$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The four conditions are the same geometric fact written in four
notational registers. Condition (a) is the informal assertion.
Condition (b) is the canonical $\varepsilon$-$K$ definition: the
absolute value formulation. Condition (c) makes the interval
structure explicit by expanding $|x_n - L| < \varepsilon$ into its
equivalent double inequality $L - \varepsilon < x_n < L +
\varepsilon$; this is useful in proofs where upper and lower bounds
are handled separately. Condition (d) is the centered interval
formulation: $x_n \in I_\varepsilon(L)$ is identical to conditions
(b) and (c) but frames convergence as set membership, which is the
natural language for the topological generalization. The index $K$
plays the same role as $N$ in the base definition
\hyperref[def:convergent-sequence]{Definition~\ref*{def:convergent-sequence}};
the letter changes here to signal that $K$ is the tail offset in
the sense of \hyperref[def:m-tail]{Definition~\ref*{def:m-tail}}.

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
The only failure mode is the existence of one real sequence with two
distinct real limits. In $\mathbb{R}$ this is impossible because
distinct real numbers can be separated by disjoint neighborhoods.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
\[
\underbrace{\exists (x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}}_{\text{some sequence}}
\;\underbrace{x_n \to L \;\land\; x_n \to K}_{\text{converges to two values}}
\;\underbrace{L \neq K}_{\text{distinct limits}}.
\]
The theorem asserts this configuration is impossible in $\mathbb{R}$.
The failure mode is not merely exotic: it occurs in non-Hausdorff
topological spaces where distinct points cannot be separated by disjoint
open sets. The proof that it cannot occur in $\mathbb{R}$ is precisely
an argument that $\mathbb{R}$ has enough room to separate any two
distinct points by disjoint $\varepsilon$-neighborhoods.
\end{description}

\;\underbrace{x_n \to L \;\land\; x_n \to K}_{\text{converges to two values}}
\;\underbrace{L \neq K}_{\text{distinct limits}}.
\]
The theorem asserts this configuration is impossible in $\mathbb{R}$.
The failure mode is not merely exotic: it occurs in non-Hausdorff
topological spaces where distinct points cannot be separated by disjoint
open sets. The proof that it cannot occur in $\mathbb{R}$ is precisely
an argument that $\mathbb{R}$ has enough room to separate any two
distinct points by disjoint $\varepsilon$-neighborhoods.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The theorem licenses the notation $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n
= L$: the definite article is justified precisely because the limit,
when it exists, is unique. Without uniqueness the limit would be a
relation rather than a function, and the notation would be ambiguous.
The proof strategy is a separation argument: if $L \neq K$ then
$|L - K| > 0$, and choosing $\varepsilon = |L - K|/2$ produces two
disjoint neighborhoods that the tail of $(x_n)$ cannot simultaneously
occupy. The Hausdorff remark in the failure mode block is the forward
pointer: when sequences are studied in general topological spaces,
uniqueness of limits is equivalent to the Hausdorff separation axiom.

inherit the same order. The proof uses the open interval between $A$ and $B$:
eventually $(x_n)$ lies near $A$ and $(y_n)$ lies near $B$, with room left
between the two tails.

nodes.name: Eventual Strict Comparison Preserves Weak Limit Order
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ be real sequences, and let $A,B\in\mathbb{R}$.
Suppose that $x_n\to A$ and $y_n\to B$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n<y_n$ for every
  $n\ge N$, then $A\le B$.
  \item If there exists $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n>y_n$ for every
  $n\ge N$, then $A\ge B$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Constant Squeeze Theorem
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence, and let $L\in\mathbb{R}$. If there
exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $L\le x_n\le L$ for every
$n\ge N_0$, then $x_n\to L$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
This is the degenerate squeeze theorem: the lower and upper barriers are the
same constant sequence. It says that eventual equality to a real number is
enough for convergence to that real number.

nodes.name: Sequence
nodes.statement_display:
Let $X$ be a nonempty set. A \textbf{sequence} in $X$ is a function
\[
    x : \mathbb{N} \to X.
\]
The value $x(n)$ is written $x_n$ and called the \textbf{$n$-th term} of the
sequence. The sequence itself is denoted $(x_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, or
simply $(x_n)$ when the index set is clear.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\forall X \neq \varnothing \;\forall x : \mathbb{N} \to X
\;\bigl(\mathsf{Sequence}(x,X) \Longleftrightarrow x:\mathbb{N}\to X\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\mathsf{Sequence}(x_n, X)
\;:=\;
x : \mathbb{N} \to X.
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A sequence is not a set of terms but a function: the index carries
independent weight. Two sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ in $X$ are equal
precisely when $x_n = y_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, so order and
repetition are intrinsic to the object. The notational collapse from
$x(n)$ to $x_n$ is conventional suppression of function-application
syntax; the underlying object remains a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$.
When $X = \mathbb{R}$, the sequence is called a \textbf{real sequence},
which is the default ambient context for this chapter.

The lower-envelope version of the squeeze principle says that eventual
two-sided order traps the eventual floors as well as the eventual ceilings.


For the alternating sequence $x_n=(-1)^n$, the tail suprema are constantly
$1$ and the tail infima are constantly $-1$, so
\[
  \limsup_{n\to\infty}(-1)^n=1,
  \qquad
  \liminf_{n\to\infty}(-1)^n=-1.
\]
For any convergent sequence $x_n\to L$, both envelopes collapse to $L$.

nodes.name: Monotone Convergence Theorem
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n)$ be a real sequence.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item If $(x_n)$ is increasing and bounded above, then $(x_n)$ converges and
  \[
    \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\sup\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
  \]
  \item If $(x_n)$ is decreasing and bounded below, then $(x_n)$ converges and
  \[
    \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\inf\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}.
  \]
\end{enumerate}

greatest lower bound of its range.

\]

$M$-tail of $(x_n)$ satisfies $P$ termwise. The index $M$ is an offset
into the sequence, not a bound on the terms themselves; two sequences
with identical $M$-tails share all asymptotic properties, differing
only in finitely many initial values which convergence arguments
discard entirely.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. The
$m$-tail $(x_{m+n})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges if and only if
$(x_n)$ converges. Moreover, in this case,
\[
    \lim_{n \to \infty} x_{m+n} \;=\; \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n.
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}

&\quad\Bigl(
    \bigl(x_{m+n}\bigr)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \text{ diverges}

\[
\bigl((x_n)\text{ diverges}\Longleftrightarrow (x_{m+n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\text{ diverges}\bigr).

Convergence is a \emph{tail property}: it depends only on the
eventual behavior of the sequence, not on any finite initial
segment. Discarding the first $m$ terms neither creates nor
destroys convergence, and when the limit exists it is preserved
exactly. This theorem formalizes the informal principle that
finitely many terms are irrelevant to asymptotic behavior. It is
the rigorous justification for the common proof move of assuming
without loss of generality that $n$ is large enough for some
auxiliary condition to hold: one simply passes to a suitable
$m$-tail, applies the argument there, and concludes for the full
sequence by this theorem. The contrapositive is equally useful:
to show $(x_n)$ diverges it suffices to show that some $m$-tail
diverges.

nodes.name: Convergence by Domination
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. Let
$(a_n)$ be a sequence of positive real numbers with
$\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0$. If there exist a constant
$c > 0$ and an index $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that
\[
    |x_n - L| \;\le\; c\, a_n \qquad \forall n \ge m,
\]
then $\displaystyle\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = L$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall (x_n) \subseteq \mathbb{R} \;\forall L \in \mathbb{R}
 \;\forall (a_n) \subseteq (0,\infty)\\
&\quad\Bigl(
    \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n \neq L
    \;\Longrightarrow\;
    \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n \neq 0
    \;\lor\;
    \forall c > 0 \;\forall m \in \mathbb{N}
    \;\exists n \ge m \;\bigl(|x_n - L| > c\, a_n\bigr)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\neq 0
\lor
\forall c>0\,\forall m\in\mathbb{N}\,\exists n\ge m
\bigl(|x_n-L|>c\,a_n\bigr).
\]


The theorem is a \emph{domination principle}: it is not necessary to
verify the $\varepsilon$-$N$ condition directly for $(x_n)$. It
suffices to find a null sequence $(a_n)$ -- one converging to zero --
that dominates the error $|x_n - L|$ on some tail, up to a fixed
scalar $c$. The scalar $c$ is irrelevant to the conclusion: since
$a_n \to 0$, the product $c\, a_n \to 0$ regardless of the size of
$c$, and any $\varepsilon > 0$ is eventually beaten by $c\, a_n$.
This theorem is the rigorous engine behind the common proof pattern
of bounding $|x_n - L|$ by a simpler expression and observing that
the simpler expression tends to zero. The canonical instance is
$a_n = 1/n$, where domination by $c/n$ is sufficient to conclude
convergence to $L$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
A failure would be a positive sequence whose consecutive ratios settle below
one in the limit but whose terms do not tend to zero. The theorem says this
cannot happen: once the ratio limit is less than one, some tail has ratios
bounded by a fixed number $r<1$, forcing geometric decay.
\end{description}

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
